Understanding the conflict four years on.

In a famous scene from Band of Brothers, the HBO epic about a U.S. paratrooper regiment in World War II, a Nazi general surrenders to U.S. forces. The Americans, rather than humiliating him, allow him to deliver a stirring address to his troops after they lay down their arms; the soldiers from both camps are visibly moved.

That incident may be exaggerated or apocryphal, but it echoed a widely held sentiment among the Allies in 1945: “In victory, magnanimity,” as Winston Churchill once summarized. But over four decades later, as the Berlin Wall fell and the Soviet Union collapsed, magnanimity was harder to come by: How much, if anything, was the United States willing to offer Russia in the wake of the Cold War?

In a famous scene from Band of Brothers, the HBO epic about a U.S. paratrooper regiment in World War II, a Nazi general surrenders to U.S. forces. The Americans, rather than humiliating him, allow him to deliver a stirring address to his troops after they lay down their arms; the soldiers from both camps are visibly moved.

That incident may be exaggerated or apocryphal, but it echoed a widely held sentiment among the Allies in 1945: “In victory, magnanimity,” as Winston Churchill once summarized. But over four decades later, as the Berlin Wall fell and the Soviet Union collapsed, magnanimity was harder to come by: How much, if anything, was the United States willing to offer Russia in the wake of the Cold War?

That question is at the heart of two books, Hubris: The American Origins of Russia’s War Against Ukraine by British historian Jonathan Haslam and Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine by journalist Stephen Kinzer. Both authors question to what extent Russia’s war in Ukraine is a reaction to decades of arrogance by the United States, full of swagger as the last superpower standing amid the ashes of the Cold War.

Hubris: The American Origins of Russia’s War Against Ukraine, Jonathan Haslam, Belknap Press, 368 pp., $25.95, September 2026, paperback

Both accounts, though overeager to blame Washington for Moscow’s belligerent turn, serve as a helpful reminder of the paths not taken in the 1990s and early 2000s, when, rather than bringing Russia into the liberal world order as a true partner, the United States encouraged rapid NATO expansion and democratization in Eastern and Central Europe, antagonizing the country.

If those decisions partly drove Moscow to move toward a break with the West, a third book, We Shall Outlast Them: Putin’s Global Campaign to Defeat the West by international relations scholar Hanna Notte, documents the culmination of Russia’s effort, showing how, since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the country has leveraged ties with allies around the globe to evade sanctions and political pressure. Alienated from the West, Russia has turned to the rest of the world. The question now is whether the West, thrown into even greater chaos by U.S. President Donald Trump’s fractious impulses, will be able to adapt.

In February 1990, soon after the fall of the Berlin Wall, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met with Western diplomats over the question of German reunification. In a phrase that has come to haunt much of post-Soviet history, U.S. Secretary of State James Baker told Gorbachev that NATO would move “not one inch” eastward if the Soviet Union withdrew from East Germany.

The flags of NATO nations are pictured during the inauguration ceremony of NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe near Paris on July 23, 1951. AFP via Getty Images

While much ink has been spilled about the meaning of that phrase—and Baker’s authorization to issue such assurances in the first place—this anticipated a pattern that would plague the U.S.-Russia relationship for 30 years. At each stage, the expansion of NATO’s membership and mission, partly at the behest of Central and Eastern European nations understandably nervous about a resurgent Russia, undermined Moscow’s perception of its own security. Ukraine would become the ultimate battleground between the forces of democratization and NATO enlargement on the one hand, and the security interests of an increasingly autocratic Russia on the other.

In the early 1990s, NATO was at a crossroads. Its raison d’être had dissolved along with the Soviet-dominated Warsaw Pact, created as a counterweight to the alliance. Haslam convincingly argues that where Western Europeans would have accepted the emergence of a post-Cold War security alliance accommodating Moscow, Washington doubled down on the status quo, which—to paraphrase NATO’s first secretary-general—meant keeping the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down.

How would NATO adapt to this unipolar moment? The answer came when the Czech Republic, Poland, and Hungary were welcomed into the club in 1999, not without significant Russian complaints. The United States ignored these grumblings, pushing for the swift admission of seven more countries in a “big bang” of expansion in 2004. NATO had just 12 members at its founding in 1949; it now has 32.

Membership was not the only thing NATO was set on expanding: It also sought a new animating impulse. Although NATO was originally framed as a defensive pact, the wars in Yugoslavia in the 1990s allowed more hawkish elements of the alliance to push for its use as an offensive force. Russia, seeing phantoms of its former self in the disintegrating Yugoslav state, vocally opposed NATO’s involvement in the Balkans, culminating in a complete break with the alliance over its unilateral bombing of Serbia in 1999.

Moscow’s inability to dissuade NATO put the Yeltsin administration in the crosshairs of nationalists on the rise at home just as the Russian economy began its free fall after the 1998 stock market crash. Both Haslam and Kinzer point to many missed opportunities in which Western powers could have bolstered Russia’s economy in its darkest hour. Instead of something akin to the Marshall Plan for Europe after World War II, Russia had to take on massive International Monetary Fund loans in exchange for painful, deeply unpopular economic reforms.

Russian navy sailors hold their passports as they line up to vote at a polling station in the Ukrainian city of Sevastopol, where the main base of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet is located, on Dec. 2, 2007. Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

Reconciliation was still feasible in the early 2000s, when Vladimir Putin became Russia’s president. In his early years in office, Putin voiced some openness to the West. Haslam details how Putin overrode members of his security apparatus to offer significant intelligence assistance to the United States after 9/11 and even approved the opening of NATO bases in Central Asia, considered Russia’s backyard, to facilitate the U.S. war in Afghanistan. Haslam argues that Washington snubbed Putin’s generosity: “Putin’s grand gesture … was effectively wasted,” he writes. The White House read it as “a desperate bid for a powerful ally against a common foe — rather than a welcome concession from a former adversary and a potential partner.”

It’s in everyone’s interest to stop the fighting. That’s still not enough.

Like a struggling swimmer, he may take desperate measures to stay afloat.

The U.S. push for regime change in Iraq, a longtime ally of Russia—and its subsequent support for revolutions in Georgia in 2003 and Ukraine in 2004—further alienated Putin. While his country could not rival the United States economically, he had other ways to put Russia back on the map. “[D]eclining powers can be at least as disruptive as rising powers,” Haslam writes, quoting William Burns, the former U.S. ambassador to Russia. “If [Putin] can’t easily build Russia up, he can take the United States down a few pegs.” Numerous foreign theaters, from Syria to Ukraine, would give him ample opportunity to try.

Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine, Stephen Kinzer, Henry Holt and Co., 384 pp., $32.99, November 2026

Both Haslam and Kinzer reach similar conclusions: that the arrogance of several U.S. presidencies, puffed up with victory in the wake of the Cold War, left them heedless to Russia’s security concerns in Eastern Europe. Neither reckons fully with Ukrainian agency, particularly with the fact that since independence in 1991, leaders of Ukraine have, of their own accord, pushed back against Russian attempts to control the country. Nor do they discuss at any length Moscow’s proactive role in fomenting trouble in its near abroad, whether through the distribution of Russian passports in breakaway parts of Georgia or by choking off energy supplies to Ukraine.

While Haslam’s approach is meticulous and relatively balanced, Kinzer, whose books have often been critical of interventionist U.S. foreign policy, clearly has an axe to grind when it comes to Ukraine. Kinzer commits to pro-Kremlin narratives and conveniently sidesteps facts that contradict them. He sees neo-Nazis everywhere in Ukraine, takes claims about the threat to Russian language there at face value, and treats the separatists in eastern Ukraine who began fighting the central government in 2014 as an autonomous force, rather than entities that were fully funded, armed, and backed by Russia from early on.

Yet both authors, in their rush to assign blame, fail to grapple with the reality that the Soviet collapse created a security vacuum in Europe. It is to some extent inevitable that Russia would feel unease at the loss of its republics, and that any moves by former allies to bolster their own security would provoke anxiety in Moscow. It is to some extent inevitable, too, that as Russia became increasingly autocratic, it would perceive any democratization nearby, including in Ukraine, as not just a domestic affair, but one with existential stakes for the Kremlin.

Of course, the war in Ukraine was not inevitable. Putin’s growing isolation, paranoia, and authoritarianism undoubtedly made a military ending to the Russia-Ukraine divorce more likely. And the hubris of the U.S. elite in the wake of the Cold War—and the whiplash created by U.S. electoral politics—meant that warning signs blinking red in the 1990s and early 2000s went unheeded, paving the way for policy that antagonized Moscow further. Many decisions could have been made differently, but even with the best of intentions, it would have been hard to resolve the fissures that culminated in the alienation of Russia from the West.

Putin addresses Western sanctions during a meeting on economic issues at the Kremlin in Moscow on Feb. 28, 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Alexey Nikolsky/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images

In the nearly five years since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has been able to pivot economically and militarily away from the West, as Notte shows in We Shall Outlast Them. With lucid and zippy writing, Notte takes us from the ports of India to the deserts of the Sahel, revealing how Russia has survived in the face of coordinated and extensive sanctions by Europe and the United States.

We Shall Outlast Them: Putin’s Global Campaign to Defeat the West, Hanna Notte, W.W. Norton & Co., 320 pp., $31.99, August 2026

Russia was still highly dependent on the Western economy as of 2022. The EU bought 50 percent of Russian oil exports and over 60 percent of its gas exports, and Western companies provided the vast majority of financing and insurance for energy shipping markets. Russia also imported one-third of its goods from the EU. Unlike the slow and uncoordinated response to the annexation of Crimea in 2014, the West moved swiftly and cohesively after the 2022 invasion, imposing price caps on Russian oil insured or shipped by Western providers and banning exports of electronics, luxury items, and dual-use goods in an effort to choke supplies.

Russia has artfully evaded these measures. In oil and gas, Russia built up a “shadow fleet” of off-the-book tankards to transport oil and evade the price cap, backed by insurers or financiers in Dubai and beyond. Russian oil exports to China and Turkey have risen, and in India alone, Russia’s share of the country’s oil imports increased from just 3 percent in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023.

For imported goods, Putin essentially established duty-free trade from third countries, allowing many European and U.S. products to enter via countries such as Turkey and Kazakhstan. Russia has pivoted towards Chinese exports and financing, decoupling its economy from the U.S. dollar (while making it significantly more dependent on the yuan). The Russian economy has certainly felt the war’s impact, with its GDP taking an initial hit before stabilizing somewhat in the years since. But it has not collapsed.

Notte also shows how Russia has navigated international diplomacy, tapping into anti-imperialist sentiment in much of the global south to position itself as the plucky outsider standing up to a hegemonic West, despite its own history of colonialism. This has paid dividends at the United Nations and beyond, where many Asian and African countries have stood with Russia in defiance of U.S. and European pressure. Where the West has sought to cut off military supplies, Russia has bolstered its alliances with North Korea and Iran, which have become major providers of munitions and drone technology. It has expanded its military footprint abroad including in the Sahel, leveraging its extensive network of mercenary groups.

A truck driver and parked trucks are reflected in a puddle outside the Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd. parking terminal in Mangaluru, India, on Sept. 5, 2025. Abhishek Chinnappa/Getty Images

Of course, there are limits to Russia’s influence abroad when it is so consumed by the war in Ukraine. In Syria, Russia could do little but watch as longtime ally President Bashar al-Assad was forced from power in 2024. Closer to home, in Armenia and Kazakhstan, Russia’s distraction militarily and economically forced these former satellites to hedge their bets and turn to partners elsewhere. Meanwhile, Moscow shored up its commitment to BRICS as an alternative to Western-dominated institutions such as the G7, but as Notte shows, the bloc’s diverse stakeholders have struggled to unite on global issues.

While Russia has avoided total breakdown, the devastation of the war cannot be understated: Aside from the economic impact, roughly 1 million soldiers are estimated to have been injured or killed, and hundreds of thousands have left the country. Russia’s autocracy has kicked into full gear, with even those voicing the mildest opposition to the war facing consequences.

In many ways, Russia’s willingness to disrupt has taken a toll not just on its own people but on the rest of the world. While many may welcome a system in which the West is no longer able to bend the globe to its will, the end of a unipolar world has so far heralded the rise of a new order that appears more fragmented, unstable, and violent. Putin has had plenty of help in this regard: Trump has done his fair share to undermine the previous status quo with his reckless gamble in Iran, his assaults on traditional allies in Europe, and his stunning betrayal of Ukraine amid the so-called diesel deal with Moscow.

Veterans of the Russian special forces lay flowers at a monument to Russian service members as they mark their professional day in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Oct. 24, 2025. Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images

Soviet leader Nikita Khruschev once famously quipped about capitalist states, “It doesn’t depend on you whether or not we exist. … History is on our side. We will bury you!” Putin has not buried the West, but he has shown how far he will go to undermine it. Putin’s regime, and Putin himself, may or may not outlive the war; as Haslam poignantly notes in closing his book, “[W]e will all sooner or later have to come to terms with a new [Russian] regime, democracy or dictatorship.” What remains to be seen is whether the collective West, whoever that may encompass by then, will have learned anything from recent history.

#5965. Talarico campaigns alongside Democrat who called ICE 'new KKK' and demanded its abolition

Fox News host Will Cain discusses accusations from James Talarico’s former classmate Mike Garcia about the Democratic Texas Senate candidate's honesty on 'The Will Cain Show.'

James Talarico, a U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, briefly praised Frederick Haynes III, a Democratic congressional candidate who compared President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts to the KKK, at a get-out-the-vote event on Thursday as part of his Clear Eyes Full Hearts tour.

"Give it up for your next congressman, Dr. Freddy Haynes. Thank you, Dr. Haynes, for those kind words and for your service to this community," Talarico said, following an introduction and speech from Haynes.

Although Talarico has not issued a formal endorsement of Haynes, the moment is notable for Talarico as he pitches himself as a Democrat who can represent the values of the Republican-leaning Lone Star State — and as he tries to distance himself from controversy over past remarks Republicans have characterized as woke.

TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE

State Representative James Talarico addresses the crowd during a campaign rally after launching his Senate campaign for the seat currently held by John Cornyn in Round Rock, Texas, Sept. 9, 2025. (Callaghan O'Hare for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Haynes, the pastor of Friendship-West Baptist Church, has framed many of his political views in the context of race and did so again on the event with Talarico.

"You transformed ICE into the new KKK and brought about terror in this nation," Haynes said of Trump's use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

"It’s time to melt ICE. It’s time to abolish ICE," Haynes added.

Haynes is running to fill the seat of Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, the incumbent in Texas' 30th Congressional District who gave up her seat in a Senate bid she ultimately lost. During his campaign, Haynes has framed his support for climate policy as a fight against "environmental racism." He has also accused conservatives and the Trump administration of benefiting from fears of Black advancement.

"They have used Black people and perceived Black progress as the boogeyman. We have not witnessed this kind of corruption, this kind of blatant corruption," Haynes said in an October interview.

"We are witnessing the demolishing of what democratic infrastructure was built by the gains of the civil rights movement," Haynes added.

Even before his congressional run, Haynes made political commentary that relied heavily on a racial lens.

After the death of Charlie Kirk, a conservative political commentator who started Turning Point USA, Haynes described Kirk as a man with views "rooted in White supremacy" and contrasted it with the deaths of Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.

"A White Christian gets killed, murdered — not assassinated. We going to tell the whole truth today. Martin King got assassinated. Malcolm X got assassinated. Medgar Evers got assassinated. Don’t compare Kirk to King," Haynes said in a September 2025 address to his church.

UN PUSHES NATIONS TO CONSIDER SLAVERY REPARATIONS BUT LEGAL GROUP SAYS IDEA 'NOT GOING TO FLY IN THE US'

Rev. Frederick Douglass Haynes III, a Dallas megachurch pastor and social activist, is running to replace Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, in Texas Congressional District 30. (Fox News)

Haynes would go on to condemn Kirk's death and political violence.

Haynes has also said he was a personal supporter of reparations.

"America, you owe us. What you done to us has been immoral. It’s been evil. It’s been unjust. It’s been downright wrong and the only way to bring salvation to America — you gotta pay us what you owe us," Haynes said at a Solidarity for Reparations event at a San Francisco church.

"I've come by to say, San Francisco, California, Texas, United States of America, if you want salvation to come to this house, you've got to engage in reparations."

For his own part, Talarico has also supported the idea of reparations, framing it as an outflow of his religious convictions.

"Reparations, repairing past harms, is part of my faith tradition. It’s part of the values I was raised with," Talarico said in a town hall meeting in July. "We have to correct the injustices of our past."

In the closing days of his campaign, Talarico has argued that, despite some of his views on race and gender which run counter to conservative stances, he could still represent Texas as a moderate.

TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS

Frederick Haynes III is running to replace outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. He is a megachurch pastor in Dallas who Crockett has cited as "my pastor." (Haynes for Congress)

"Our campaign has been able to show that you can be a more moderate, reasonable candidate and still be exciting," Talarico said in October.

Talarico’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment if his comment about Haynes should be viewed as an endorsement of his platform or his views on race in politics.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

#5964. Union boss stuns with major Republican endorsement as election nears

Sen. Ashley Moody criticizes Democratic opponent Angie Nixon over her remarks about Cuba and capitalism on 'The Faulkner Focus.'

The leader of one of the nation’s oldest and largest unions stunned political observers by issuing a surprise endorsement for a Senate Republican stalwart over the weekend.

Teamsters General President Sean O’Brien, who famously nearly came to blows with now-Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin during a Senate hearing before ultimately becoming acquaintances, issued a ringing endorsement of Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., signaling a major break from national union sentiment that has tended to favor Democrats.

"Just voted in the State of Florida for the first time, and very proud to have cast a ballot for Sen. Ashley Moody," O’Brien, whose 123-year-old union is about 1.3 million-strong, announced Sunday.

5 TAKEAWAYS FROM FLORIDA SENATE PRIMARY: GOP SEN ASHLEY MOODY WILL FACE DSA'S NIXON

"Sen. Moody has been extremely helpful working with the Teamsters to protect workers’ pensions, defend good-paying jobs, and support well-funded union apprenticeship programs."

"The Teamsters look forward to working with Sen. Moody in her role on the Senate HELP Committee to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act and get this critical legislation signed into law to protect American workers," he added.

FRUSTRATED BLUE-COLLAR UNION BOSSES RIP SOCIALIST POLITICIANS, WARN OF LABOR EXODUS FROM DEM PARTY

O’Brien, a self-described "lifelong Democrat," previously spoke at the 2024 Republican National Convention, but emphasized at the time that the Democratic Party had snubbed his request to speak at its convention.

"If the far-left want to criticize me and attack me, that’s OK. If the far-right wants to do the same, that’s great. I represent 1.3 million hardworking men and women," O’Brien said at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Teamsters as well as Moody’s campaign for comment.

Moody, a former state attorney general, said in a statement that she was proud to have O’Brien’s endorsement:

"I’ll always fight to protect hardworking Americans, strengthen good-paying jobs, and ensure resources are available to train our next generation. It’s been great to deliver for Florida’s working families," she said.

After O’Brien endorsed Moody, the lawmaker’s Democratic opponent responded by posting a photo she once took with O’Brien and writing that "Ashley Moody never walked the line with you."

AOC BACKS FLORIDA DEM ANGIE NIXON FOR US SENATE: 'I’M PROUD TO ENDORSE HER'

Sean O'Brien, general president of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, speaks during a press conference outside the West Wing of the White House on Oct. 30, 2025, in Washington, D.C., flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. (AFP via Getty Images)

"But ok brother. Shout out to all the rank and file Teamsters that are voting for me. I will always stand with you," Democratic nominee Angie Nixon, a state lawmaker from Jacksonville whose platform is considered DSA-aligned, wrote on X.

O’Brien also caught heat for voting in Florida, which appeared to signal a move from his hometown of Boston.

DSA candidate Angie Nixon advanced to a high-profile November Senate matchup against Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. (Nixon: Joe Raedle; Moody: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)

"Be union leader — move to a famously anti-union state — vote for a famously anti-union candidate — Brag about it — really cool stuff man," a top commenter on O’Brien’s post said. Other critics characterized O’Brien as a "scab", union jargon for someone who crosses a strike picket line to return to work for the company with which they are at odds.

The Teamsters leader’s announcement marked a noteworthy development with polls set to open nationwide in a matter of hours.

#5963. The World’s Biggest Crypto Heist

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: The World’s Biggest Crypto Heist

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an alleged North Korean cyberattack on Binance, Israel’s parliamentary election results, and mixed NATO messaging on Russia’s threat to Europe.

Hackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange late Thursday, stealing more than $6 billion in under 30 minutes. Experts are calling it the biggest crypto heist in history, and initial investigations suggest that North Korea is to blame.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at an alleged North Korean cyberattack on Binance, Israel’s parliamentary election results, and mixed NATO messaging on Russia’s threat to Europe.

Hackers targeted the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange late Thursday, stealing more than $6 billion in under 30 minutes. Experts are calling it the biggest crypto heist in history, and initial investigations suggest that North Korea is to blame.

According to U.S.-based blockchain research firm TRM Labs, an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor targeted $6.36 billion in Binance digital coins spread across 10 blockchains. The hackers were unable to access consumer accounts, instead only affecting Binance corporate holdings. Around $3 billion in assets have already been located or frozen, but TRM Labs estimates that the hackers had moved roughly $2.4 billion in crypto coins “beyond any issuer’s reach.”

“Your assets are safe,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on Friday in a statement intended to ease customers’ concerns. However, analysts argue that the heist—despite its limited impact on consumers—has exposed the risks of trading crypto as well as the growing prowess of North Korean hacking efforts.

Cryptocurrency is a relatively new phenomenon in the world of economics—and one that is still largely unregulated. In June 2024, then-presidential candidate Donald Trump vowed to make the United States the “crypto capital of the planet” if elected for a second term, and since then, he has focused on reducing aggressive oversight of the lucrative industry. He also launched his own cryptocurrency platform, World Liberty Financial, which is run by his two sons, as well his own meme coin cryptocurrency.

Some countries, such as Russia, have turned to cryptocurrency to help evade sanctions and procure sensitive dual-use goods. Crypto companies have also faced a slew of cyberattacks. In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency accused North Korean hackers of stealing roughly $1.1 billion in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the course of five years. Such hackers came under scrutiny again in February 2025, when the FBI said that TraderTraitor stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, one of Binance’s top rivals. And last month, attackers took around $350 million from cryptocurrency exchange Bitget.

A Binance spokesperson told The Associated Press on Friday that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.” However, TRM Labs said that its analysts had “high confidence” in the company’s assessment that the North Korean hacking group is responsible.

“North Korean hackers are among the world’s most aggressive and highly skilled cyber actors,” former South Korean Vice Defense Minister Shin Beom-chul told the Financial Times on Friday. Last year alone, Pyongyang’s hackers stole around $2 billion in cryptocurrency, accounting for roughly 60 percent of total crypto heists in the world, according to estimates from blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

Bitcoin’s value plummeted more than 5 percent overnight Thursday into Friday in response to the Binance heist, and other cryptocurrency exchanges dropped as much as 9 percent.

Israel’s coalition talks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have lost their parliamentary majority, final election results confirmed on Friday. Although Netanyahu’s Likud bloc still has the most seats in the Knesset, a historic showing by unaligned Arab parties means that lawmakers likely have several weeks of intense coalition-building negotiations ahead of them before a new government can be formed. In the interim, Netanyahu remains in charge.

According to the final results, Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc won 53 seats, main opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party-led alliance won 48 seats, and Arab-led groups won a record 19 seats. If Eisenkot wants to dethrone Netanyahu, then he will likely need to ally with the Arab parties to secure a majority. However, Eisenkot may be loath to do so, as one of his key partners, right-wing lawmaker Avigdor Lieberman, has ruled out joining a coalition with the predominately Arab Joint List or Raam parties.

Netanyahu has capitalized on such hesitance, accusing Qatar of funneling money into Israel to support the Arab vote. Israel’s elections committee said the “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless,” and the Qatari government dismissed Netanyahu’s accusations as “ridiculous and dangerous.” Yet Israeli intelligence agency Shin Bet has promised to investigate the claims.

Pentagon messaging on Moscow. The Trump administration has urged several NATO members in recent weeks to water down their rhetoric regarding the threat that Russia poses to Europe, Reuters reported on Friday. Sources said that senior U.S. defense officials, including Defense Department policy chief Elbridge Colby, have urged Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania to dial down their warnings, arguing that they are not helpful for ongoing peace talks. Russian hybrid warfare, including drone incursions, has hit all three NATO members in the past year.

U.S. negotiators are reportedly considering new incentives to end the Russia-Ukraine war, including possible sanctions relief for and business deals with Moscow. Last week, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff held separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin; during talks with Putin, Witkoff called the Russian leader a “humanitarian” and announced that negotiations would soon begin on the technical level.

The report about the Pentagon’s urgings also came on the same day as a G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attended in person. Deep rifts among the attendees prompted U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to cancel the group’s traditional family photo, as many participants balked at standing beside Lavrov. Several European leaders have accused the Trump administration of being too soft on Moscow.

Global port strike. Dockworkers in 22 countries went on strike on Friday to protest the use of ports for arms exports and, specifically, for the delivery of weapons to active war zones. More than 25 unions across 113 ports—from Southern Europe to North Africa and India—backed the protests, which are in support of the so-called Istanbul Declaration, a document signed in May by dockworker unions from more than 35 European ports that demands an end to arms shipments from their sites.

“From planes to tanks, guns to bullets, explosives to ammunition, uniforms to boots, our ports have become replenishing and forwarding bases for war and ⁠genocide,” ​unions said at a press conference held to announce the strike. The Global Sumud Flotilla, a pro-Palestinian maritime activist group that has repeatedly tried to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza to deliver humanitarian supplies, also vowed to support ​Friday’s movement.

It is unclear how disruptive the 24-hour demonstration might be. Organizers said that the strike could impact more than 40 percent of Mediterranean cargo and around $2 billion worth of freight. However, shipping experts suspect that global trade will not be significantly hurt. Still, FP energy reporter Keith Johnson told World Brief that the strike “is more sand in the gears of a global economy already strained by U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade wars and real wars, both of which have sent freight rates to nosebleed levels this autumn.”

How did right-wing presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro react to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s runoff election victory on Sunday?

A. He graciously conceded defeat. B. He called for his followers to protest his loss in Brasília. C. He fled to Chile. D. He said he would request an annulment of the election.

For a small sum of $56 million, you too can be the owner of a famous Impressionist painting. Claude Monet’s Iris became the most expensive artwork sold at auction in France last Thursday. The massive canvas, depicting some of Monet’s favorite flowers in his Giverny garden, is part of a 20-piece series produced near the end of the artist’s life. It took the title of most expensive work sold at a French auction from sculptor Amedeo Modigliani’s Head ⁠of ​a Caryatid, which sold for around $48 million in 2010.

D. He said he would request an annulment of the election.

Lula became the first Brazilian presidential candidate in history to come from behind to win the election’s second round, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports. Bolsonaro, the subject of several criminal probes, subsequently fled to Miami, where he called himself “the leader of Brazil.”

#5962. The Israel Netanyahu Made

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DALIA DASSA KAYE is a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania and a Senior Fellow at the UCLA Burkle Center for International Relations.

Why Bibi’s National Security Vision Will Endure

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has dominated his country’s politics for the last four decades, and his influence will not end even if Israelis vote him out of office. Over the course of his tenure as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu has dramatically reset the terms of the country’s national security politics. His persistent rejection of Palestinian statehood has helped push the idea firmly out of mainstream debates, and his longtime agitation for war against Iran is now widely accepted policy across Israel’s political and security establishment.

Before his first term as prime minister, Netanyahu was already a divisive figure. In 1993, as the leader of the opposition, he likened Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s Oslo agreement with Palestine Liberation Organization leader Yasir Arafat to British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain’s appeasement of Hitler ahead of World War II. His inflammatory rhetoric emboldened Israelis who considered any territorial compromise with the Palestinians to be treasonous, including the assassin who killed Rabin in 1995. Today, extreme policies and positions have become normalized under Netanyahu’s watch. He has presided over a three-year campaign of mass destruction and displacement in Gaza and the killing of more than 70,000 Palestinians. His government includes one politician, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was barred from serving in the army in his youth because of his involvement in terrorist groups, and another, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has said Israel needs “to wipe out Gaza” and that it should repeat what it “did in Gaza” in the West Bank. Defense Minister Israel Katz has made similar calls for applying the “Gaza model” to the West Bank and even southern Lebanon.

Netanyahu might soon lose power. His attacks on Israel’s judiciary, corruption trials, and refusal to take responsibility for security lapses ahead of Hamas’s terror attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, have generated significant opposition among Israelis. A change of leadership could have profound consequences for domestic policy. But whether Netanyahu leaves politics this week or years down the road, his national security vision will outlast him. He has had catastrophic success in crushing domestic support for Palestinian national aspirations and gaining mainstream backing for a permanent war footing to confront Iran. Netanyahu has changed the baseline of how Israelis think about their country’s security and turned his own uncompromising positions into an institutionalized reality. Future leaders may bring their own styles to Israeli security policy, but for the foreseeable future, at least, they will be coloring within lines that Netanyahu has drawn for them.

Netanyahu is not the first Israeli prime minister to reject Palestinian national aspirations. In a 1969 interview, Golda Meir famously asserted that there was “no such thing” as a distinct Palestinian nation. Menachem Begin embraced the 1978 Camp David accords with Egypt only because the agreement did not require him to come to terms with the Palestinians. Yitzhak Shamir refused to allow independent Palestinian representation at the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference.

The difference today is that the idea of Palestinian statehood is not even up for debate. This change did not happen overnight. Rabin’s assassination led to the dismantling of the Oslo model, which intended to produce a Palestinian state but in practice produced limited Palestinian self-government and continued Israeli control over much of the West Bank. Attacks by Palestinian terrorist groups throughout the 1990s deepened Israelis’ skepticism about the prospects of peace, which helped to bring Netanyahu to power in 1996.

Still, when Netanyahu’s first term ended in 1999, some politicians sought to keep the possibility of a political settlement alive. Israelis elected leaders such as Ehud Barak and Ehud Olmert who were open to territorial concessions to the Palestinians and who engaged in serious, albeit unsuccessful, U.S.-backed peace negotiations. Barak also spearheaded a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon in May 2000. Even the hawkish Ariel Sharon, whose controversial visit to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem later that year helped spark the second Palestinian intifada, evacuated around 9,000 Israeli settlers and initiated the withdrawal of ground forces from Gaza in 2005.

But in the absence of a negotiated solution, the conflict worsened on all fronts. Hamas won the 2006 elections in Gaza and took full control of the territory by 2007. Military conflict between Israel and Hamas became routine, with major wars erupting in 2008, 2012, 2014, and 2021. Netanyahu became prime minister again after the first of those wars, in 2009. As Israel contended with frequent rocket fire from Gaza and missile attacks by the Lebanon-based Hezbollah in the north, Netanyahu linked the deteriorating security conditions to Israel’s earlier withdrawals from these areas, bolstering his case against territorial compromise.

Netanyahu’s policies also changed realities on the ground in the West Bank. Even before his return to power, after the second intifada broke out, Israel built a concrete wall to separate Israel from the West Bank that encroached substantially on internationally acknowledged Palestinian territory. Israeli checkpoints throughout the West Bank also severely limited Palestinians’ freedom of movement and access to East Jerusalem. In office, Netanyahu accelerated policies, including continued settlement expansion, that threatened the viability of a future Palestinian state. And he encouraged a growing divide between Hamas in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank by facilitating Qatari payments to Hamas-run Gaza for more than a decade, further undermining the Palestinian national project.

Even the coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that briefly removed Netanyahu from power from 2021 to 2022, and which promised change, did not substantially depart from Netanyahu’s positions. It is telling that this coalition—the only one able to push Netanyahu aside in the last decade and a half—boasted strong right-wing security credentials; Bennett was a longtime opponent of Palestinian statehood. Rather than taking steps to advance peace with the Palestinians, Bennett and Lapid focused on the Abraham Accords, the agreements negotiated by the first Trump administration in which several Arab states committed to normalizing relations with Israel without requiring concrete progress toward Palestinian statehood in return.

Few vocal supporters of Palestinian statehood remained within the political establishment on the eve of October 7, 2023. The attacks that day all but ensured that opposition to a Palestinian state would become the norm. No Israeli political leader, even in the opposition, speaks anymore about ending Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank. After destroying much of Gaza and killing tens of thousands of Palestinians, Israel has regained military control of nearly 70 percent of the strip. Israeli settlers in the West Bank, whose numbers have more than doubled since the Oslo accords were signed, have been attacking Palestinians with alarming frequency. The settlers have ravaged Palestinian villages as the Israeli government and military look the other way, if not outright condone the violence. Palestinians, as a result, are now more focused on survival than statehood. Whether Netanyahu wins or loses this election, there is no clear path to the two-state future he has been so determined to avoid.

Netanyahu’s hardline position on Iran has been just as consistent as his hardline attitude toward the Palestinians. As early as 1992, as a member of the Knesset, he warned that Iran was “racing to develop nuclear weapons” and that the “threat must be uprooted.” More than three decades later, Netanyahu finally found in Donald Trump a U.S. president willing to launch the military campaign against Iran he had long sought. The first attack went forward in June 2025, when the United States and Israel struck key nuclear sites in Iran. Then, on February 28, they began a larger war targeting the Iranian leadership itself. As Netanyahu announced in a video message at the start of hostilities, “Together with the U.S., we will strike the terror regime hard and create the conditions that will enable the brave Iranian people to cast off the yoke of this murderous regime.”

The Israeli public and Israeli politicians expressed near-uniform support for the war in its early months; Lapid, the leader of the opposition, declared it a “just war.” By June, polls showed more public criticism of Netanyahu’s handling of the war. But few Israeli politicians have questioned the need to maintain military pressure on Iran, and active planning for renewed attacks continues. When Yair Golan, the leader of the left-wing Democrats party, called Israel’s killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khameini a “mistake” that led to an even more extremist Iranian leadership, politicians across the political spectrum condemned him.

There used to be more debate among Israel’s military, intelligence, and political elite about how to deal with Iran. When Netanyahu’s government began seriously considering a conventional military strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities in 2012, for instance—a development that drew concern in Washington—Israeli leaders did not all immediately coalesce around the idea of attacking Iran. Notable voices such as Meir Dagan, the former head of Israel’s intelligence agency, the Mossad, were arguing against a military strike and questioning what such a move could accomplish. The debate over military options became moot, however, once the Obama administration announced an interim nuclear deal with Tehran, negotiated in 2013 via back-channel diplomacy through Oman. The deal surprised and infuriated Netanyahu, who tried without success to scuttle the final nuclear agreement, which was signed in 2015.

Netanyahu’s strident opposition to U.S. President Barack Obama’s diplomacy was not supported by all Israeli politicians, either. Many worried that campaigning against the nuclear deal would damage Israel’s relations with Washington and that Netanyahu’s growing alignment with the U.S. Republican Party threatened bipartisan support for Israel. Although the Israeli government officially opposed the agreement, several prominent political leaders and members of the security establishment argued that the deal could have upsides. Benny Gantz, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, called the deal an “achievement” that could postpone Iranian nuclear capabilities for ten to 15 years. Some Israeli officials even argued against a U.S. withdrawal from the deal when Trump, with Netanyahu’s enthusiastic support, threatened to do so without first establishing an alternative arrangement. Even Barak, who had supported military strikes on Iran in the past and criticized the nuclear deal when it was signed, questioned whether Trump’s pulling out of the agreement was the “optimal” way to deal with Iran.

But these debates largely dissipated after Trump withdrew from the deal in 2018. When Iran resumed its nuclear enrichment program and with diplomatic efforts at a dead end, Netanyahu seized the opportunity to renew Israel’s shadow war with Tehran. Explosions at Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility in July 2020 and April 2021 were widely attributed to Israeli intelligence, as was the killing of Iran’s top nuclear scientist in November 2020, after the election of U.S. President Joe Biden, who had promised to restore the nuclear deal during his campaign. Even when the Bennett-Lapid coalition took over, Israeli positions on Iran remained consistent. The new government was less confrontational than Netanyahu’s, but it opposed a U.S. return to the nuclear deal. Bennett argued, as Netanyahu had done before, that an agreement would channel funds into “the Iranian terror machine.”

After October 7, with Netanyahu back in power, Israel escalated its attacks on Iran and its proxies. These actions included strikes in Tehran and Beirut that killed the heads of Hamas and Hezbollah, as well as tit-for-tat missile exchanges with Iran in April and October 2024. Aside from criticism that Netanyahu was timing the attacks to serve his own political interests, opposition figures such as Lapid and Gantz supported Netanyahu’s actions and the public backed what had become open military confrontation between Israel and Iran.

Israeli leaders have rallied behind Netanyahu’s preference for military confrontation over diplomacy, and not only with Iran. The idea that preventive military action should be used to manage any potential threat has guided Israel’s campaigns not only in Palestinian territories but also in southern Lebanon and in Syria after the fall of the Assad regime. Israel has been crossing new lines: it launched its first military attack on a Gulf Arab state in September 2025 with an airstrike in Doha targeting Hamas leaders. War has become Israel’s normal state of affairs.

Even if Netanyahu loses power, Israel’s approach to national security is unlikely to change. The opposition has articulated clear differences from the current government on matters of domestic policy, but major fissures on the Palestinian conflict, Iran, and Israel’s wider regional military campaigns are less apparent. As many Israeli analysts have put it, the political spectrum of the opposition is in essence “50 shades of right.”

Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival, might slow settlement expansion in the West Bank and crack down on settler violence if he becomes prime minister. But those steps would amount to tactical adjustments, not strategic shifts. Eisenkot is not suggesting that Israel end its occupation of the West Bank or make a serious effort to advance a two-state solution. He has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional” in the wake of October 7. Other leading opposition figures, such as Bennett, not only oppose a Palestinian state but also avidly support settlement expansion.

A new government would not overhaul Israel’s policy in Gaza, either. There is widespread resentment among opposition politicians and the Israeli public over how Netanyahu waged the war, especially his resistance to cease-fire agreements that could have saved the lives of more hostages. Many believe Netanyahu prolonged the war to stay in power. But there is far less concern about the war’s effect on Palestinians; only a small number of Israeli human rights groups say Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. An Eisenkot government might be more inclined to advance the stalled Trump peace plan for Gaza, which has yet to make meaningful progress on reconstruction, Palestinian governance, or other key objectives. But like Netanyahu, Eisenkot does not support giving up Israeli control of Gaza without the full disarmament of Hamas.

More fundamentally, Israeli leaders across the board now consider control of territory to be essential to national security—whether in Gaza, the West Bank, southern Lebanon, or Syria. As the Middle East scholar Nathan Brown has observed, to the extent that debate about Israel’s security doctrine remains, it “is increasingly about how Israeli predominance should be exercised, not whether it should be maintained.” A new government might be willing, with Washington’s backing, to strike a nonaggression agreement with Syria that would require the removal of Israeli forces from border areas. Many leading Israeli politicians oppose such a withdrawal, however, lowering the odds of a deal going through. And it is even less likely that Israel would cede ground anywhere else.

No major Israeli politician is arguing for a change of course on Iran. The only significant domestic criticism of Netanyahu’s Iran policy has been about his failure to prevent diplomatic agreements, such as the short-lived memorandum of understanding the Trump administration reached with Tehran in June, which most Israelis see as favoring Iran and as failing to remove Tehran’s nuclear and missile threat. Israeli military leaders are already planning for the next round of war, including for a possible scenario in which Israel has to fight Iran on its own. Maintaining this war footing seems to have broad political support, too. Lapid has argued that Israel should go even further in its attacks on Iran, including by bombing “all energy facilities” to make sure the “Iranian economy is demolished.”

Netanyahu would have found it far more difficult to bring his hardline vision into the mainstream had he faced a political opponent who could powerfully advocate for a fundamentally different vision for Israel’s place in the region and path to peace. There have been no Rabins in the Israeli opposition, no leaders willing to pivot from their own previous positions, tell the public the truth about what a real peace would require, and invest in the painstaking work of diplomacy. Instead, Netanyahu’s governing style has stifled robust debate on national security questions and lined up Israel’s defense leadership behind the prime minister’s own uncompromising worldview that favors continuous reliance on military force.

Neither did Netanyahu face serious pushback from Washington as he pursued policies that thwarted any hope for peace with the Palestinians, including the relentless destruction of Gaza. Even though U.S. public attitudes toward Israel have grown increasingly unfavorable, on both sides of the political divide, American presidents have become less willing to use diplomatic and economic leverage to cajole Israeli leaders to end dangerous activities such as settlement expansion. The lack of pressure from the United States—and some Arab states’ willingness to normalize relations with Israel without demanding serious progress toward reconciliation with the Palestinians—made it easier for Netanyahu to pursue hardline policies without making concessions. It weakened dissenting voices within Israel, too, who could not convincingly criticize those policies on the grounds that they would damage Israel’s security or relationships with its most important partners.

Of course, regional realities complicate Netanyahu’s worldview. The plight of the Palestinians continues to resonate with foreign publics, limiting how far pivotal countries such as Saudi Arabia will go in normalizing relations with Israel. Yet future Israeli leaders may not be overly concerned about that problem, convinced that Israel, with its military might and technological edge, has too much to offer potential partners to be ignored or isolated. Many Israeli politicians today are dismissive of the increasingly common view in the region that Israel is as great a security threat as Iran.

A serious reversal of Netanyahu’s security policies will not be possible until a new Israeli leader emerges with a bold alternative plan for how Israel achieves lasting peace—and with the ability to bring the Israeli public on board. And as long as the United States remains Israel’s closest political and security partner, helping this shift along will require U.S. policies that stop enabling and start pushing back on Israeli settlement expansion, territorial occupation, and reckless military escalation.

None of this is happening during the current Israeli election season. In fact, there is little chance of it happening any time soon. Netanyahu has triumphed in squashing Israeli support for Palestinian national aspirations and normalizing military confrontation with Iran. It’s a powerful legacy. But it is not one that will make Israel, the region, or the world better off.

Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens faces intense party backlash after endorsing Republican candidate Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the heated Michigan Senate race.

House Democratic leaders are holding off on deciding whether to punish Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., after she endorsed a Republican in Michigan's Senate race, drawing calls from fellow Democrats for her removal from the party's House caucus.

Stevens endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., over Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, on Nov. 1 — just two days before Tuesday's midterm elections.

The decision prompted sharp criticism from Democrats, including lawmakers who want Stevens expelled from the House Democratic Caucus, but party leaders are waiting until after the elections to address her future.

HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION'

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and U.S. Senate candidate, and Rep. Haley Stevens, a Democrat from Michigan, speak to members of the media following a service at Perfecting Church in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A senior Democratic aide told Fox News Digital that House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., would likely support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., in his response to Stevens' endorsement.

"Haley Stevens made a terrible decision, blindsided everyone and isolated herself from the House Democratic caucus. We will have a discussion about appropriate next steps upon our return," Jeffries told POLITICO.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Aguilar did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Stevens, a four-term lawmaker, is leaving Congress at the end of the year after narrowly losing Michigan's Democratic Senate primary to El-Sayed.

Since her loss, Stevens has taken a lukewarm approach to supporting El-Sayed’s campaign while also criticizing his approach to Israel and Jewish and Black voters.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries speaks alongside Rep. Pete Aguilar and Rep. Katherine Clark during a news conference in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 8, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

That fragile peace ruptured over the weekend when El-Sayed’s campaign publicly asked Stevens to abstain from appearing at any of his events even after she said she would attend church with him and Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., in a bid to mobilize Black voters.

Stevens apparently blindsided fellow Democrats when she then appeared at another church alongside Rogers and his wife and subsequently endorsed the Republican ahead of Election Day.

EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE

Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said during a Sunday appearance on CNN that Stevens had reassured her "multiple times" over the weekend that she would not endorse Rogers.

"I don't know what changed between late Saturday and Sunday morning," Dingell said during another CNN appearance Monday.

And the endorsement also spurred her ouster from the Michigan state Democratic Party.

Michigan Democratic Party Chairman Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens "is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future" after she backed Rogers.

In the House, Democratic officials, such as Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., have already called for Stevens’ removal.

"Deplorable and embarrassing. Capitulating to fascism, Islamophobia, racism and the policies hurting everyday Americans makes you unfit to serve with the Democratic caucus," Ramirez wrote on X. "Shame on Haley Stevens. She must be removed from the caucus."

Ramirez did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed takes questions from reporters after a campaign rally on Oct. 24, 2026, in Detroit. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News Digital)

Vocal organizations aligned with the Democratic Party, such as the IfNotNow movement, have also formally called on the congresswoman to be removed from the caucus, calling her endorsement a betrayal to the party.

"As national organizations representing Jewish, Muslim, and Democratic voters opposed to Donald Trump's war on Iran, which is responsible for the rising costs of gas and groceries and an affordability crisis that is taking a heavy toll on working families at a time when the future of our democracy is at stake," the organization said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "We call on House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries to expel Congresswoman Stevens from the Democratic Caucus and strip her of her committee assignments."

If Stevens was removed from the caucus, she would no longer be able to attend its weekly meetings in the U.S. Capitol. Democrats could also pursue action against her committee assignments, though the process and authority for doing so would need to be determined under the applicable caucus and House rules.

#5958. Putin’s Strategy Is Working

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MICHAEL MCFAUL is Professor of Political Science, a Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute, and a Hoover Fellow at Stanford University. He served as Ambassador to Russia from 2012 to 2014 and is the author of Autocrats vs. Democrats: China, Russia, America, and the New Global Disorder.

Trump Could Salvage the Kremlin’s Objectives in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin plays the long game. For decades, the Russian leader has worked to subjugate Ukraine. For decades, he has also cultivated ties with Donald Trump. Now, success at the latter endeavor is allowing Putin to recover from failures at the former: after nearly five years of thwarted Russian objectives in the war on Ukraine, the U.S. president is helping him win. By easing sanctions on Russia, cutting military and economic assistance to Ukraine, disrupting intelligence cooperation, and pressuring Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to accept Putin’s war aims, Trump is making Russia’s successful annexation of substantial Ukrainian territory and de facto control over Kyiv’s future decisions more likely than at almost any point since February 2022.

Since Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine, battlefield momentum has swung back and forth between the two sides. Russian forces had the advantage at the start. But by the fall of 2022, Ukraine had seized the offensive, liberating so much territory once held by Russian troops that Washington worried Putin might use a nuclear weapon to stop Ukrainian advances. The war then settled into a tragic grind on the frontline—until last spring. Momentum returned to Ukraine after Kyiv deployed new long-range missiles capable of striking targets deep inside Russia, new midrange drones able to attack Russian supply routes in the occupied parts of eastern Ukraine, and improved interceptor drones that could better defend against Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities. Putin’s army proved unable to advance on the frontline; Ukrainian troops even made incremental progress in liberating territory.

But Trump has helped return the momentum to Russia. Stymied at the frontline, Putin has shifted his focus to terrorizing Ukrainian society through rocket and drone strikes on both civilians and the infrastructure their livelihood depends on—energy and water in particular—driven by the hope that a suffering population would pressure Zelensky to capitulate. New weaponry has made this terrorist campaign especially brutal, in particular the mass production of ballistic missiles and a new drone, the Geran 5, equipped with a powerful Chinese rocket engine that Ukrainian air defenses cannot intercept. Because Russia has more troops, greater military production capacity, and some new and better weapons, Putin believes that he can afford to persist despite the seeming stalemate.

Trump’s support has bolstered Putin’s belief that time is on his side. In just the last few weeks, Trump and his allies have expanded his help to Moscow: suspending sanctions, buying Russian diesel, disrupting Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems, and even insisting that Zelensky must go. “It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia,” Zelensky has noted, “it only reinforces Putin’s belief that his goals are within reach.” The combination of less support from the United States, especially when it comes to air defenses, and faster Russian drones and more missiles will make the coming winter the most brutal yet for Ukrainians.

Putin’s long game with Trump began years ago, driven not so much by some specific objective, but by the hope that Kremlin influence on him might someday prove useful—a common KGB tactic. Now that day has come.

Years before Trump first ran for president, Russian actors close to Putin pursued business ties with the then real estate mogul, including most famously when Trump collaborated with Emin and Aras Agalarov to host the Miss Universe pageant in Moscow in 2013. Putin then orchestrated unprecedented foreign interference in the 2016 presidential election to help Trump and hurt his opponent Hillary Clinton. Whether the Russian theft and publication of Clinton campaign emails, combined with a comprehensive social media effort to bolster Trump, affected the 2016 election outcome is impossible to prove. That Putin was trying to influence the result is without question.

In 2017, Putin’s cultivation of Trump started to deliver some atmospheric benefits. Trump made clear his admiration for the Russian dictator. More shockingly, during his summit with Putin in Helsinki in 2018, Trump expressed doubt about the findings of his intelligence community regarding Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and instead endorsed Putin’s denial. Yet in his first term, Trump’s rhetorical adulation of Putin only marginally changed actual U.S. policy toward Russia, in part because several senior officials on Trump’s national security team—National Security Adviser H. R. McMaster, Secretary of Defense James Mattis, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo—constrained Trump from making a full pro-Russia pivot.

After Trump’s reelection, in 2024, the Kremlin’s long courtship started to produce more tangible results. Most consequentially, Trump ended direct U.S. military and economic assistance to Ukraine. Before then, the United States was Ukraine’s biggest backer. Trump has still allowed American companies to sell some arms to European governments, who then transfer them to Ukraine. But even that channel has been disrupted periodically and only amounts to a trickle of weapons and ammunition compared with what the United States previously provided. And what Ukraine needs most—interceptors for its Patriot missile defense systems—are in very short supply, in part because the United States has launched so many of them during Trump’s war with Iran.

Other U.S. steps have further undermined Ukraine and aided Russia. Trump has insisted that Ukraine would never join NATO. He gave Putin red-carpet treatment at an Alaska summit last year, at which the two presidents talked about pressuring Ukraine to give up the rest of the eastern region of the Donbas, which Putin has been trying to conquer since 2014. Trump has periodically berated Zelensky, including most dramatically at a February 2025 Oval Office meeting, when he cut off Zelensky and yelled, “You’ve done enough talking. You’re not winning this . . . You don’t have the cards.” Since then, Trump has occasionally zagged back to more cordial relations with the Ukrainian president. But Trump has returned to expressing open hostility, echoing Putin by proclaiming that it’s “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

In the last two weeks, Trump has increased support for Putin’s war. He lifted sanctions to allow the sale of Russian diesel exports, which will provide Moscow with billions of dollars to help finance military operations. He issued an executive order suspending new sanctions outlined in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he had signed just weeks earlier. There have been new lapses in sharing certain kinds of intelligence that only the United States can provide. Most consequentially, Ukraine has experienced disruptions in its access to Starlink and Starshield communications systems provided by SpaceX (a company owned by Elon Musk, a major backer and ally of Trump and a former official in his administration). Kyiv needs both services to guide its own drones and to track and defend against Russian drones and rockets. Whether the U.S. government or Musk independently ordered the disruptions is still not clear. But the results of the disruptions were clear: more Russian drones and rockets hit more Ukrainian targets, including innocent civilians; more Russian weaponry moved closer to the frontline; and more Ukrainian drones fell out of the air.

Through their teams, Putin and Trump have also been negotiating new business deals, including the purchase of assets owned by a major Russian oil company, Lukoil, by American investors; the sale of a currently dormant gas pipeline, Nord Stream 2, connecting Germany and Russia; and even secret Russian investments in a liquefied natural gas project in Alaska. If they move forward, all these projects will provide Putin with new revenues to underwrite his war in Ukraine.

Ukrainians are not giving up; according to polls, a solid majority still think that their country should keep fighting. Nor are Europeans quitting on Ukraine. Although Putin hoped that the withdrawal of American military and economic aid early in Trump’s second term would lead to a quick Ukrainian collapse or capitulation, he did not anticipate how willing and capable European countries would be in filling the American void. What’s more, Ukrainian defense tech companies are working frantically to develop new weapons to intercept the rapidly rising number of Russian ballistic missiles and speedy Geran 5 drones. Right now, the pendulum has swung in Russia’s direction, but the Ukrainians have defied expectations and regained momentum many times in the past; they can do it again.

U.S. policy could also change, especially after the midterm elections. American society does not support Trump’s embrace of Putin and abandonment of Ukraine, making it politically hard for the administration to maintain this policy pivot. If Democrats win control of one or both houses of Congress in midterm elections next week, they could very well use their new electoral mandate to investigate American-Russian business deals; introduce new legislation to restart American military and economic assistance to Ukraine and outlaw Starlink and Starshield disruptions; or deploy legislative action to enforce existing sanctions laws. Even Trump himself has stepped back from Putin before—he once wondered out loud whether Putin was “tapping me along.” He could do so again.

Putin should also realize that his cultivation of Trump is a wasting asset. No future president—Democrat or Republican—is likely to continue Trump’s Russia policy. And next week, Trump will become a lame duck, whose power to shape U.S. policy toward Russia will decline over the next two years. Putin would be wise, accordingly, to get serious about negotiating a cease-fire now. His odds of getting a favorable deal will only diminish from here.

#5957. The Biggest October Surprise of All

Analysis: The Biggest October Surprise of All
