Since Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise Oct. 25 reelection victory, global attention has focused on his opponent, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio—the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022—promptly fled to the United States, where he declared himself the “leader of Brazil.” The younger Bolsonaro is under criminal investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering.

Flávio’s departure from Brazil will have consequences for the country’s right. But for now, the more intriguing question is about the future of Brazil’s left. Lula turned 81 on Tuesday. Although he is fresh off an electoral triumph, he will need to start cultivating viable successors immediately—a task that he has struggled with in the past.

Since Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise Oct. 25 reelection victory, global attention has focused on his opponent, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio—the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup after losing to Lula in 2022—promptly fled to the United States, where he declared himself the “leader of Brazil.” The younger Bolsonaro is under criminal investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering.

Flávio’s departure from Brazil will have consequences for the country’s right. But for now, the more intriguing question is about the future of Brazil’s left. Lula turned 81 on Tuesday. Although he is fresh off an electoral triumph, he will need to start cultivating viable successors immediately—a task that he has struggled with in the past.

Lula’s political resilience and longevity are unmatched by most democratically elected politicians. He first ran for president in 1989 and won on his fourth attempt, in 2002. After two presidential terms lasting from 2003 to 2010, a corruption conviction kept him out of the 2018 race that brought Jair Bolsonaro to power. Brazil’s Supreme Court annulled Lula’s conviction in 2021, and he defeated Bolsonaro the following year by less than 2 points. Lula won his fourth term in the contest against Flávio by roughly twice that margin. Since Brazil’s redemocratization in the 1980s, no other politician has been elected president more than twice.

Lula has shown a remarkable ability to adapt to new political realities and change his policy programs without losing his base. In government, he has traditionally moved to the center, building coalitions with parties that share few positions with his Workers’ Party (PT). His first vice president in the early 2000s was a textile mogul who helped assuage concerns among economic elites about Lula’s candidacy. His current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, was the center-right presidential candidate whom Lula beat in the 2006 runoff. Whenever out of power, Lula has returned to lead the left—and occupied that space so that no rival could emerge.

Those who tried to challenge Lula and the PT’s dominance on the left have failed spectacularly. Marina Silva, Lula’s environment minister from 2003 to 2008, left the PT and became a serious presidential contender in 2014 under the banner of the Brazilian Socialist Party. She ran on a platform that combined a progressive social agenda with market-friendly economics.

When polls showed that she was likely to win a runoff against President Dilma Rousseff—Lula’s chosen successor—the PT aired vicious television ads against Silva. Her candidacy never recovered. In 2023, while in office for a third time, Lula brought her back as environment minister.

Ciro Gomes, who served as minister for regional development in Lula’s first cabinet, attempted to run for president in 2010. Yet Lula maneuvered to keep his governing coalition united behind Rousseff, and Ciro’s own party dropped his candidacy. Four years later, the PT drew the Gomes family back in, with Ciro’s brother serving as Rousseff’s education minister. Lula’s strategy has been consistent: contain and weaken the rival, then bring them or their allies back into the fold.

That method has kept Lula at the center of Brazilian politics for four decades. It also deprived the left of anyone who had the national visibility to succeed him. For years, the PT’s best-known alternative candidate was Fernando Haddad, who served as education minister under both Lula and Rousseff and, until March, as Lula’s finance minister. But he has now lost four elections in a row: for reelection as mayor of São Paulo in 2016, for president in 2018, and for governor of São Paulo in 2022 and again this month.

Lula will have to address his succession problem in what is likely to be the most challenging of his four terms. Starting in February, the Bolsonaro-backed Liberal Party will hold 121 of 513 seats in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies and 28 of 81 seats in the Senate, making it the largest caucus in both. That will make it hard for Lula to pass legislative priorities or get Supreme Court nominees confirmed.

According to the International Monetary Fund, Brazil’s fiscal deficit will be close to 8 percent of GDP this year. Gross public debt stands at above 80 percent of GDP, by the central bank’s measure—and at above 90 percent by the fund’s assessment. That leaves very little room for the spending increases that Lula promised during his campaign. U.S. tariffs on Brazil remain in force, and with the Strait of Hormuz still under threat, oil prices climbed above $115 a barrel this month, feeding energy costs and inflation across Latin America.

Lula is thus bound to face high public rejection rates from day one. And since, as an incumbent, he won’t have the honeymoon period that recently elected presidents usually enjoy, he risks becoming a lame duck early. A president governing under these constraints has every incentive to keep power close. Yet Lula’s political legacy—and the left’s capacity to remain competitive without him—now depend on him doing what he has avoided throughout his career: letting others grow and, ideally, outshine him.

Lula’s one previous attempt at developing a successor was not encouraging. Choosing Rousseff to run for the presidency in 2010 was perhaps the gravest political error of his career. Rousseff had previously served as energy minister in Lula’s first government and later became his chief of staff. But she had never run for office, lacked the skills to work with Congress, and pursued an interventionist economic program that helped produce a deep recession.

Brazil’s GDP fell 3.5 percent in 2015 and 3.3 percent in 2016, its worst two-year stretch in more than a century. Rousseff was impeached that year. After a period of commodity boom-fueled growth and optimism, the economic downturn led to widespread discontent and ultimately opened the way for Bolsonaro to win in 2018.

Lula is hardly alone in mishandling a potential successor. Former U.S. President Joe Biden tasked Vice President Kamala Harris with addressing the root causes of migration from Central America, an assignment with few chances of visible success. That made it harder for her to be competitive when he withdrew from the 2024 race.

Now, Lula should build a bench instead of anointing an heir. There are several younger politicians in the PT and allied parties who could become nationally known and tested over the next several years.

The most obvious candidate is Rafael Fonteles, the 41-year-old governor of Piauí. Elected in 2022 at the age of 37, he became the youngest governor in the state’s history after serving as its finance secretary from 2015 to 2022. He belongs to the PT’s more market-friendly wing. This month, he was reelected with 70.9 percent of the vote. Piauí now has the lowest homicide rate of the nine states in Brazil’s northeast. After losing the first round of the presidential race to Flávio, Lula put Fonteles in charge of his campaign’s communication—which markedly improved as a result.

If Fonteles left the governorship, Lula could make him finance minister, a post now held by Dario Durigan, who replaced Haddad in March. The ministry would expose Fonteles to the national and international business communities and increase his name recognition. The downside of serving as finance minister is that the next four years will require the government to make unpopular economic decisions, and Lula would have to make sure that whoever gets the job does not absorb all the political cost.

The Foreign Ministry is an alternative: Fonteles is known to have a keen interest in international affairs and has actively sought to attract foreign investors to Piauí. Making him foreign minister would carry fewer risks and be an opportunity to present a younger, progressive Brazilian leader to the world.

Camilo Santana, a two-term governor of the state of Ceará and former education minister, leads the PT in the Senate. At 58 years old, he was the political coordinator of Lula’s runoff campaign. João Campos, 32, of the Brazilian Socialist Party, and Renan Filho, 47, of the centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement, both lost governor’s races this month. Ministry posts would keep both in national politics; Lula himself has mentioned Campos as a possible candidate for 2030. Durigan is in his early 40s, but as a technocrat, he lacks a base of his own.

Giving key ministerial posts to all these contenders would be difficult. Countless allies of the president—including Haddad; former PT President and Federal Deputy Gleisi Hoffmann, who until this year was Lula’s chief negotiator with Congress; and Rio de Janeiro Mayor Eduardo Paes—lost their election races and may expect Lula to give them positions in his cabinet.

Rather than specifically aiming to nurture leaders for the presidential contest in 2030, Lula should view his succession strategy as a long-term project to keep the PT competitive. Given pervasive anti-incumbency sentiment and little hope for sufficient economic growth to offset it, the right is favored to win Brazil’s presidency four years from now—particularly since the scandal-ridden Bolsonaro family appears to have exited the political scene. Unless a new generation of left-wing leaders can use Lula’s final presidential term to gather executive experience, progressive forces risk being the underdogs for several electoral cycles.

Whoever emerges as Lula’s successor will inherit a party that is difficult to manage and that many voters reject outright. In a March Ipsos-Ipec survey of Brazilians, 27 percent cited the PT as their preferred party, and 37 percent said they would never vote for the party.

The PT is also split between a hard-left wing and a social-democratic one. The party’s relationship to Venezuela under former President Nicolás Maduro provided a vivid example. Hoffmann, who led the party from 2017 to 2025, attended Maduro’s 2019 inauguration and described the country’s 2018 presidential vote as legitimate—well after Maduro had become authoritarian. She and Haddad, a leading member of the social-democratic camp, clashed over the trip.

A future candidate will have to constantly manage these tensions without being seen as flip-flopping or opportunistic. But Lula must give them the space to grow. Unless he provides a new generation with the opportunity to gain national and international visibility, the Brazilian left is bound to become an underdog.

Oliver Stuenkel is a senior fellow in the Democracy, Conflict, and Governance Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington, D.C., and an associate professor of international relations at the Getulio Vargas Foundation in São Paulo. X: @OliverStuenkel

#5945. Pentagon's top spies tasked with 'no-fail' mission as Hegseth puts foreign midterm meddling in crosshairs

President Donald Trump adds campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas after previously canceling them. Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt discusses the president’s 2026 midterm campaign blitz and the administration’s energy policy.

Ever since the 2016 presidential election that first got President Donald Trump elected and the ensuing Russiagate scandal, there has been increased scrutiny on foreign meddling in U.S. elections and threats to the American voting system.

Now, 10 years later, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is directing his entire intelligence and spy forces to ensure foreign adversaries do not interfere in Tuesday's midterms.

The Pentagon chief has ordered America's military intelligence and cyber agencies to mobilize against foreign threats to the 2026 elections by directing his department's sprawling intelligence apparatus to make election security a priority in what he calls a "no-fail mission."

The September directive reaches beyond U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency, instructing the entire Defense Intelligence Enterprise — including agencies responsible for military and geospatial intelligence — to "mobilize every authorized asset, capability, and partnership" against foreign election threats.

HOW TO WATCH CRITICAL 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RACES IN TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME AND FL

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth addressed reporters during a Pentagon news conference in Arlington, Virginia, on June 26, 2025. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The order puts some of the military's most sophisticated intelligence capabilities behind a mission that has grown considerably since Russia's interference in the 2016 presidential election. But with Americans preparing to vote, the extent to which Hegseth's directive has changed the Pentagon's existing election-security operations remains unclear.

The Department of War declined to provide Fox News Digital with additional details about how the order is being implemented. Cyber Command separately declined an interview request about its election-security efforts.

In practice, the directive can mean military intelligence agencies are tasked with identifying foreign hackers or influence operations overseas, warning civilian agencies about threats headed toward U.S. targets and, when authorized, Cyber Command taking action against the foreign actors or infrastructure behind them.

The military's role largely stops at the U.S. border: state and local officials run elections, while agencies such as the FBI and Department of Homeland Security handle the domestic side.

The Pentagon's election security mission is not new. Cyber Command and NSA have spent years tracking and disrupting foreign threats around American elections, including operations targeting Russian actors during previous election cycles.

The effort began taking its current shape ahead of the 2018 midterms, when the agencies formed a "Russia Small Group" focused on foreign interference. It later evolved into a joint Election Security Group, combining NSA's intelligence-gathering capabilities with Cyber Command's ability to conduct operations against foreign cyber threats.

An election official sorts ballots during early voting, Oct. 28, 2025, in Portland, Maine. (Robert F. Bukaty/AP)

By 2022, then-Cyber Command and NSA chief Gen. Paul Nakasone was describing election security as an "enduring, no-fail mission" — language echoed by Hegseth four years later.

"Rest assured, we were doing operations well before the midterms began, and we were doing operations likely on the day of the midterms," Nakasone said after the 2022 election, describing the military's role as "understanding your foreign adversaries and operating outside the United States."

The agencies again established an Election Security Group for the 2024 presidential election, but whether that structure was recreated for this year's midterms has been less clear.

Gen. Joshua Rudd, the current head of Cyber Command and NSA, told lawmakers in April that foreign interference was "reasonable to expect based on what we've seen in the past" and said his command was "postured and ready to support as required or tasked." He said at the time that he was unsure whether the Election Security Group had been reconvened.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Five months later, Hegseth issued his department-wide directive, addressed not only to Cyber Command and NSA but also to the directors of the Defense Intelligence Agency and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

The order instructs military intelligence agencies to collect and analyze intelligence on foreign election threats while directing Cyber Command to use its existing authorities and capabilities to counter potential foreign cyber activity in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security.

It does not publicly grant new authorities or establish a new election-security organization, instead reinforcing a mission the military has increasingly treated as an enduring responsibility.

U.S. intelligence officials, meanwhile, say they have seen no evidence that a foreign adversary has attempted to interfere with voting machines, physical election infrastructure or the counting of votes ahead of Tuesday's midterms.

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member of the House Intelligence Committee, said last week that intelligence officials continue to see nothing contradicting that assessment, but urged Americans to remain "on high alert" for foreign disinformation, particularly as artificial intelligence makes such campaigns easier to spread.

But officials continue to track foreign influence efforts from Russia, China and Iran, with Russia remaining the most active foreign influence threat, CNN reported Sunday.

In this photo illustration, the names of the presidential candidates, including former President Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris, appear on a vote-by-mail ballot on Oct. 2, 2024, in Miami, Florida (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

U.S. elections are attractive targets for foreign adversaries because the stakes extend far beyond who wins office: influencing American voters or undermining confidence in the process can shape U.S. policy, weaken public support for policies they oppose and deepen divisions without ever touching a voting machine.

Lawmakers briefed on classified intelligence last month said Russia was using disinformation to target candidates and undermine confidence in the election, while China's influence efforts were more narrowly focused on candidates viewed as hostile to Beijing.

The Pentagon's role focuses on threats originating overseas, while state and local officials administer elections and civilian federal agencies lead domestic election-security efforts.

Hegseth's directive makes that overseas mission a priority across the broader military intelligence enterprise, though the Pentagon has not disclosed whether it has resulted in additional personnel, resources or organizational changes ahead of Election Day.

#5943. Only the Gulf Can End the Iran War

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALLISON MINOR is a Senior Fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and served as Deputy U.S. Special Envoy for Yemen from 2021 to 2023.

NATE SWANSON is a Resident Senior Fellow and Director of the Iran Strategy Project at the Atlantic Council. He served as Director for Iran at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2025. In the spring and summer of 2025, he served on the Trump administration’s Iran negotiating team.

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

For everyone involved, the war in Iran has been a strategic failure. The United States and Israel have shown that they can achieve a few military objectives, such as sinking Iran’s navy. But after eight months of fighting and pressure, they have also proved that they cannot forcibly realize their main ambitions, including regime change, destroying Iran’s nuclear program, or even reopening the Strait of Hormuz—a waterway that was not closed when the war began. The Islamic Republic, for its part, has demonstrated that it can survive intense bombings. Yet it cannot break the American military’s economically suffocating blockade and has thus far failed to achieve its goal of putting an end to indefinite threats of war against Iran.

In theory, the war’s descent into a painful stalemate should open the door to diplomatic outcomes. But both sides have proved incapable of making the concessions necessary to strike a deal. Instead, they appear to prefer a mutually destructive status quo that maintains the delusion of achievable victory and which they can justify with the continued pain they inflict on their adversaries. As a result, rather than moving toward a settlement, both sides are threatening renewed attacks.

But there is a face-saving way for Iran and the United States to extricate themselves from this conflict: a cease-fire brokered and managed by the Gulf Arab states. The deal would begin with Gulf countries providing economic relief to Iran in exchange for Iran lifting its restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz. This would, in turn, allow the United States to lift its own blockade. The Gulf states would also need to commit to taking steps to deter Washington from resuming strikes on Iran in the future. But neither the United States nor Iran would need to make direct concessions to the other, and each would avoid the most painful compromises. The United States, for example, would not have to lift its “maximum pressure” campaign, and Iran would not have to agree to limit its nuclear program. Gulf states could then use their leverage to sustain the cease-fire until conditions permit a more comprehensive agreement.

Serving as the guarantor of a cease-fire comes with real costs and risks for the Gulf, but its countries have good reason to accept them. They are part of the battlefield on which the Iran war is being fought, and should the conflict continue indefinitely, it could pose a threat to the very economic and political models on which they are built. The Gulf depends on oil and gas exports to sustain itself, and there is no way it can completely bypass the Strait of Hormuz in shipping its energy resources abroad. Its efforts to diversify away from hydrocarbons, meanwhile, are also vulnerable to renewed attacks from Iran.

Securing a cease-fire will not be easy. It requires that the Gulf countries overcome their own lack of cohesion, that Iran prioritize economic recovery and forgo explicit guarantees about U.S. behavior, and that the United States gives Gulf countries the space necessary to reach a deal. Even if successful, the resulting agreement will not address the underlying issues driving the war. But with scant alternatives on the horizon, it is the best—and perhaps the only—way to ease the pain for everyone.

In theory, a U.S.-Iranian agreement should be straightforward. There is a historical template for deals between Iran and the United States—Tehran agrees to constrain or give up a specific behavior, and Washington agrees to give it money and recognition—that could apply neatly to the current conflict. In the Algiers Accords of 1981, for instance, Iran agreed to release American diplomats it held hostage in exchange for frozen funds and a commitment by the United States not to intervene in Iran’s internal affairs. In the 2015 nuclear deal, Tehran accepted strict limits on its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief and an implicit acceptance of its right to enrich uranium. Today, Iran could stop impeding maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (and perhaps eventually make concessions on its nuclear program), and Washington could grant it some combination of sanctions relief, cash, and acknowledgment of Tehran having a formal role in the waterway.

In practice, however, reaching this understanding will be extremely difficult. One reason is technical: Iran won’t make the nuclear concessions that U.S. President Donald Trump wants, and the United States will not provide the upfront, irreversible financial incentives that Tehran demands. But the bigger problem is reputational. To justify his quixotic war and decision to withdraw from the 2015 nuclear deal, Trump wants sweeping concessions from Tehran. Iran, for its part, is loath to settle for fewer benefits than it received from the United States in their ill-fated June memorandum of understanding, in which Washington pledged significant relief. As a result, both sides feel compelled to sustain the confrontation, even though doing so is mutually detrimental.

The Gulf states cannot resolve the dispute over Iran’s nuclear program. But they can bring about relative peace by helping address other essential issues. The United States may not be willing to pay Iran for merely opening the Strait of Hormuz, but its Gulf partners have the wealth and the motivation to offer the regime immediate economic concessions. Those partners could, for instance, give Iran some form of humanitarian and reconstruction funding. Iran, in turn, would stop attacks on ships transiting the strait and on Gulf states themselves. In response to Iran ceasing its attacks on commerce, the United States would lift its own blockade, and the Gulf states and Iran would establish a temporary deconfliction mechanism for shipping that acknowledges Iran’s role in the waterway without establishing unacceptable precedents for international commerce. This mechanism could require that ships use Iran’s preferred traffic pattern but would not formalize Iranian control over the passage.

This particular arrangement would not resolve Iran’s other core objective—prohibiting the United States and Israel from launching a renewed military campaign. This concern is harder to address. The United States may lack a credible military endgame, and the war might be unpopular domestically, but that has not stopped an erratic Trump from drawing up plans for renewed military action. But the Gulf states can provide Iran with assurances that they would use their leverage with Washington to help deter future attacks. For example, in May, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia temporarily paused U.S. access, basing, and overflight—the approvals that allow the United States military to use Gulf countries’ territory and airspace—because of concerns about the United States’ plans for escorting merchant ships through the Strait of Hormuz. The tactic worked: the United States paused the operation.

The United States might bristle at handing Iran negotiations over to the Gulf countries. But ultimately, U.S. officials should be able to spin this deal as a win. Trump, for instance, could exit the war while telling Americans that he saved the world from high energy prices without making the kind of economic and nuclear concessions to Iran that the Obama administration did under the 2015 agreement. He could likewise boast about the steps he took to weaken Iran, and, in the absence of a nuclear deal, point out that his self-proclaimed “maximum pressure” sanctions remain in place. In fact, in some ways, a Gulf-brokered deal is exactly the kind of “America first” foreign policy Trump promised. It would let the region take on the burden of managing a bad actor, including responsibility for providing most of the necessary concessions. Trump would have stumbled into the outcome. But he would still leave office with an empowered set of allies more capable of managing their own security.

Iran, for its part, would not only get significant economic benefits. It might also advance its goal of reducing the United States’ influence in the region. After all, if Israel or the United States undermines an arrangement down the road, it will only accelerate the decline of Washington’s credibility and influence with its Gulf partners. The United States has already placed its relationship with these countries under stress by going to war with Iran, something they did not ask for and for which all have suffered serious consequences. A Gulf state deal would thus allow Tehran to leverage any future U.S. military campaigns against Iran to further drive a wedge between the United States and its regional partners.

Iran has repeatedly made clear that its top war-related priority is to end the war on terms that reduce the likelihood of a future conflict. To some extent, Iran has already achieved this benchmark with the pain it has inflicted on the global economy. Assuming this war eventually ends, the next time an Israeli prime minister asks an American president to approve an attack on Iran, that president will have to weigh global economic instability against Israeli security interests. The threat posed by Iran, in the absence of a nuclear breakout or massive terrorist attack, may not outweigh the risk to the global economy. Israel might act independently of the United States, but doing so would risk further damaging the U.S.-Israeli relationship and invite Iranian retaliation without American protection.

But this deterrent is effective only once the current iteration of the war ends. If the war continues, Iran will forfeit the future de facto security guarantee that the Strait of Hormuz and geography provide. The longer this conflict goes on, the more it favors those in Israel or the United States advocating for regime change or endless war. Unless there is a solution to high energy prices that allows Trump to disengage from Iran, he will continue grasping, and it could eventually lead him to adopt aggressive kinetic options that have not yet been tried—and for good reason.

Iran and the Gulf countries are already exploring regionally led solutions to the conflict. On October 26, Saudi officials traveled to Tehran to meet with their Iranian counterparts, alongside leaders from Pakistan and Turkey. Gulf countries had also planned to meet with Iran in Salalah, Oman, on September 14 to discuss the Strait of Hormuz. But that gathering never happened, and unless there is a broader regional solution, Gulf countries will instead mostly pursue private, bilateral deals with Iran to help forestall future attacks on their ships or territory. These agreements might help lessen the pain for individual Gulf countries in the short term, but they fail to address the overall risk of Iranian escalation or resolve the global consequences stemming from disputes related to the Strait of Hormuz. Furthermore, they allow Iran to stoke division and distrust between Gulf countries while driving up its own demands.

To get a workable deal, the Gulf states will thus need to improve internal cohesion. This is easier said than done, particularly in light of continued tensions between two of the major Gulf players—Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. But fixing this issue is wholly within the power of Gulf states, and the Salalah effort demonstrates there is some interest in doing so. Improving cohesion among Gulf states also does not require resolving the larger bilateral tensions and competition among the region’s capitals; it only requires an agreement to isolate the Iran issue from those tensions and address this shared imperative. The Gulf states must therefore collectively agree on redlines for Iranian behavior and coordinate on how to enforce them. If Iran seeks to test the agreement or demand more concessions from Gulf governments, they must collectively push back by pausing economic aid or cooperation—even if it means risking Iranian retaliation.

The Gulf states and Iran will also be tested by the Houthis. Saudi Arabia understandably holds Iran accountable for Houthi attacks on its territory because Iran helped build the group’s capabilities, continues to provide it with significant technical and material support, and helped trigger the re-escalation of the Yemen conflict in July. But Iran does not control the Houthis, so the group is not going to stop attacking Saudi Arabia or call off its campaign inside Yemen simply because Iran says to. Tehran will thus need to extend an olive branch to Riyadh by showing that it is willing to limit its direct involvement in the current Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia. For instance, Iran could credibly promise Riyadh that Tehran-backed Iraqi militias will stop attacking the kingdom. It was, after all, Iraqi militia attacks that took the kingdom’s valuable East-West oil pipeline offline on September 10, and defending against attacks from both the north (where Saudi Arabia borders Iraq) and south (where it borders Yemen) greatly complicates Riyadh’s already strained air defenses.

These efforts to craft a deal might still come up short. Even if the Gulf states overcome their internal divisions and sideline concerns about Houthi activity, Tehran and Washington could refuse to sign on. Iran could conclude that control of the strait and the ability to throttle energy markets are its best security guarantee, whereas the United States might struggle to even implicitly acknowledge that the war will not achieve the outcome its leaders promised. And even if the cease-fire agreement does work, the result will be far from ideal, for both the United States and its Gulf partners. It could encourage Iran to increase its control over the strait, and it could weaken U.S.–Gulf state partnerships. Worse yet, it fails to address the underlying issues driving the U.S.-Iranian conflict and the tensions between Iran and its neighbors: Tehran’s nuclear program and support for armed groups, respectively.

But a comprehensive Iran deal is not feasible today. A Gulf-brokered outcome on the Strait of Hormuz is. In fact, it may be the only way to stop a mutually hurting stalemate that is poised to last years and cause mounting damage to global markets. The strategies that states have employed to blunt the consequences of global oil and gas shortages will likely start wearing thin in 2027, as governments deplete their strategic reserves, Chinese demand increases, and alternative supply routes out of the Gulf come under Iranian attack. The economic consequences of the conflict could even undermine the domestic stability of the most vulnerable Gulf states or reignite old conflicts, as happened in Yemen this year. A Gulf-brokered deal, then, is the least bad outcome. Such is the irony of this conflict: the bystanders that have already lost the most will need to save the warring parties from themselves.

#5942. A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

Argument: A New USAID Can Be Smarter and Sharper

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

“A very good morning,” I said in Spanish, smiling at the young director of the Colombian National Land Agency as we exchanged congratulatory handshakes. It was 2024, and my U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) team and I had just arrived to inaugurate new offices for the land agency in downtown Bogotá, where fresh staff and IT systems would help speed the laborious and typically yearslong process of turning paperwork into official land titles.

It had taken years of hard work and millions of dollars of aid to bring reform to Colombia’s dysfunctional land administration system, in which more than 40 percent of rural landowners lacked proper titles. Over several years, we had carefully researched ownership in several key counties, and now it was the land agency’s turn to convert our surveys into official titles.

Looking at the elaborate setup, I turned to my program manager and asked under my breath, “How much did we pay for this?” USAID contractors always footed the bill for such events, in my experience. “Nothing,” he replied. “This is their show.”

This memory epitomized for me both the promise and dysfunction of my 21 years at USAID. We existed to bring such transformational reform to life, within the governments of our host countries. Yet we were hampered by our own systems and practices.

The end of USAID’s operations in September 2025 was a tragedy—for U.S. soft power and influence, for the lives in developing countries that have been lost, and for the shameful treatment of USAID’s foreign and American staff. But the agency was not perfect, and as we look toward building back something better, we need to think sharply about how to make a system more interested in transformation than paper-clip counting.

I recognized much of what frustrated me with USAID in the pages of Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s 2025 bestseller, Abundance—too much paperwork, pursuing low-risk and low-impact approaches when we knew better ones, and stymied by process over outcomes.

USAID generally spent its funding through competitively awarded grants and contracts to NGOs and for-profit contractors. These entities would, in turn, hire experts, rent out offices, and buy vehicles and equipment to provide expertise to the host-country organization.

In this case, our contractor was a big, for-profit U.S. firm. Staffed by very capable Colombians, it was always a struggle to get our contractors to see why the real goal was for the local government to take over. The contract required deliverables, such as 20,000 land titles issued, not the deeper reforms that the inauguration of the new offices represented.

The whole system of measurement and incentives within USAID worked against these moments. Our standard indicators counted units, such as the number of people trained, but had no way to measure transformation. The auditors were notorious for only finding fault and lack of compliance, not handing out kudos. Nothing in any of our systems awarded us for the host country, rather than ourselves, taking on responsibility for a project.

These are not entirely new questions. In former USAID Administrator Andrew Natsios’s widely read 2010 essay, “The Clash of the Counter-Bureaucracy and Development,” he detailed how USAID had become consumed by compliance and paperwork, spending “as much money on oversight and control as on implementation.” Worse, it had strayed from its mission of creating transformational partnerships with developing countries in favor of low-risk, countable outputs.

I moved to Washington in 2000 and worked as a management consultant for federal agencies until 2004, when I became a foreign service officer with USAID. The practices and acronyms Natsios described were our bread and butter—inspector general audits, performance measurement, and strategic planning. I naturally carried that skillset over when I began my USAID career. My last tour was as deputy director in Colombia, the largest USAID program in the Western Hemisphere. As I became a senior USAID officer, Natsios’s critique rang truer and truer to me.

A perennial directive during my 21 years at USAID was to push us, working in the field missions, to work more with local partners. Most recently, the goal of former Administrator Samantha Power’s localization initiative was to provide 25 percent of USAID’s total funding in direct contracts and grants to local partners. The Biden administration ended with still a long way to go to meet that goal, reaching only 12 percent of funding.

The development theory was simple; partners more involved in designing and managing programs would produce more sustainable programs that they saw as their own, not as the donor’s. To be sure, done poorly, there were plenty of potential downsides to giving direct grants to local partners, such as heightened corruption, aid dependency, and exacerbating local power dynamics as local elites would often control this funding.

But there were other potential advantages, too. Locals tend to understand how to get things done in their own country and may devise more appropriate solutions, and grants to local partners often cost less to implement.

Despite all these efforts, most of our funding went to grants to large international NGOs, the United Nations, or to big contracts with for-profit firms that had developed around implementing specialized USAID funding, known as “Beltway bandits.” Most USAID staff instinctively knew that local partners would have a better angle on problems. But we also knew that it was just too complicated and time-consuming to do it at scale.

Natsios described the situation in 2010 as one where the complexity of working with USAID, “restricted newer, smaller, and local organizations from competing for grants and contracts, because these organizations lack the business systems to follow U.S. federal law and regulation, to account properly for all funds, to disburse money quickly, and to produce measurable and auditable results.”

In 2025, 15 years after Natsios published his essay, the situation was about the same or perhaps marginally better with regard to the proportion of USAID funding globally going to local organizations, probably increasing by a couple of percentage points, from 10 to 12 percent.

In Colombia, the proportion going to local organizations was far less than the global average—only about 5 percent of our funding went to local partners. The rest went to large international NGOs, the U.N., and Beltway bandits. Speaking as someone partly responsible for this situation, this was insane.

Colombia, while having significant development challenges and needs, is considered by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development to be an upper-middle-income country. It has a highly developed private sector and state. The challenges noted by Natsios of “lack of business systems” were much less an issue in a place such as Colombia, yet we provided very little of our funding to local partners. Our complicated design and contracting processes were the same whether the grant was $100,000 or $10 million, disincentivizing smaller projects—while USAID’s complexity put off local partners. We had clear incentives to spend but no penalties for not working with locals. And we had the staff to manage 20 large grants but not 100 small ones.

When I ask myself how we could move from the bureaucratic, risk-averse, and process-focused USAID to a new and redesigned foreign assistance that is bold and transformative, my answers stem from my own experience—and the limited number of projects I felt were truly successful. In my 21-year career, I probably worked on or led just five or six projects I would consider to be absolutely transformative out of dozens of projects. Other work was good, but it did not have the same feeling of real change.

I felt that difference powerfully one night in Kabul in 2016. We were running a virtual online auction at the U.S. Embassy, where private sector investors from around the world would bid on a new 10-megawatt solar farm project in Kandahar. The CEO of the Afghan utility and his senior staff accompanied us in person, and we watched on a TV monitor as bids came in from companies. The numbers slowly got better and better as the night progressed. When bidding closed, the Afghan government had a deal at a world-class price from the winning company.

This moment meant that the Afghan government could negotiate with the global private sector, equal to equal, without donors as intermediaries. The teary-eyed CEO hugged me and immediately called the Afghan president to tell him the good news.

No standard indicator can capture that moment, and it was not featured as a headline in the next audit report. Yet that moment was so transformative that this approach to infrastructure was repeated to great effect by the Afghans on their own. The Afghan government used the private investor approach we piloted with them that night to triple the output of Kajaki Dam with Turkish investors over the next few years.

Models exist within USAID and federal foreign assistance to pull from. Down the hall from me in Bogotá sat the lead for USAID’s Office of Transition Initiatives (OTI) program. I was envious of the fact that she wasn’t there that often but instead out in the field working directly with communities on small infrastructure or community projects. OTI’s model was completely different than the rest of USAID. Field managers were expected to be in the field, bonding with counterparts, adjusting programs, and making things happen. Back-office contract and finance work was done in Washington. If I wanted to get a read on the political dynamics at a key counterpart agency, my first stop was to speak to the OTI rep.

The Inter-American Foundation (IAF), a much smaller U.S. federal body, also worked with those small communities and NGOs doing truly grassroots development work. In Colombia, it worked with small Indigenous-led NGOs serving their community or women’s groups helping them to start small businesses—organizations often without offices or full-time staff.

How did IAF do it? Its procedures were completely different from ours, its funding scale was generally under $100,000, and it included a key condition in making these grants. It generally requested that an NGO’s own contribution be at least as much as IAF’s, ensuring that this was the NGO’s project and the NGO owned it.

Global problems are landing on U.S. shores in unprecedented numbers. The right focuses on migration and illegal drugs, while the left sees climate change and pandemics. However you weigh each of these threats, they could all be mitigated by well-designed foreign assistance.

I know this is the case because I managed such programs in Colombia just prior to the mission’s closure. We helped Venezuelan migrants take advantage of generous policies that would allow them to stay in Colombia, rather than start their hike to the United States through the Darién Gap. Other programs incentivized coca farmers to stop growing coca and make their livelihood legally. Climate finance preserved hundreds of thousands of acres of virgin forest to slow climate change. Funding helped Colombia’s health ministry prepare for the next pandemic. Foreign assistance is not a panacea but remains an essential tool to protect the United States.

As Natsios reminds us, development is about building institutions “in poor and fragile states, with the ultimate goal of developing a capable state, market economy, and civil society.” It’s not about bean-counting. It is time to think boldly about how we could redesign foreign assistance around that objective and help solve the threats facing the United States.

Jeremiah A. Carew was the deputy mission director of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in Colombia from 2021 until the mission’s closing in August 2025. Over his 21-year career with USAID, he served in Peru, Afghanistan, Uganda, Vietnam, South Sudan, and Washington, D.C. He retired at the rank of counselor in the U.S. Senior Foreign Service, and his final assignment was as mission director of USAID in Somalia. He currently resides in Ecuador, where he writes on international development topics for Razón Pública in a monthly column; his work has also appeared in El Tiempo and the Foreign Service Journal.

#5940. Battleground Dem touts bipartisan record, but can’t name single issue she’d work with Trump on

Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan told Fox News’ Bill Melugin she is more concerned about the Trump administration’s "continued grift" than finding common ground with the president.

A Democratic Senate candidate in Minnesota touted her bipartisan record Sunday but could not name a single issue she would work with President Donald Trump on, instead accusing his administration of "continued grift."

The exchange came as Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, Minnesota’s Democratic Senate nominee, campaigns against Republican Michele Tafoya in a race Republicans see as a rare opportunity to flip a traditionally blue state. Flanagan’s answer underscored the sharply partisan nature of the Minnesota race, where she has cast Tafoya as a rubber stamp for Trump and pledged to oppose the administration at nearly every turn.

"I just want to be really clear that I’ve got a long track record of working with folks on the other side of the aisle," Flanagan told Fox News' Bill Melugin when asked if there were any policies she could see herself working with Trump on. Flanagan pointed to her work at the Children’s Defense Fund–Minnesota and her time in the Minnesota Legislature, where she served alongside a Republican majority and helped pass bipartisan legislation, as evidence of her ability to work across the aisle.

"I think that, you know, that proves that I have the ability to work with folks," she continued.

PEGGY FLANAGAN DEMANDS EXPANDING THE SUPREME COURT AND ABOLIHING ICE

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, speaks during a primary election night party on Aug. 11, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minn. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

Flanagan’s bipartisan pitch comes against the backdrop of a campaign built around opposing Trump’s agenda. She has called for dismantling ICE, passing Medicare for All, and reversing the administration’s Medicaid and SNAP cuts, while accusing Trump of using the presidency to enrich himself.

"Right now, I’m deeply concerned about the Trump administration, the continued grift, making money hand over fist directly from the Oval Office," she continued in her response to Melugin on whether she would work with Trump on anything.

The Democratic Senate candidate went on to tell Melugin that what she has been "hearing" on the campaign trail is that voters want someone who will be a "check" on Trump, not his ally.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign rally at Rock Hill Sports and Event Center on Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026, in Rock Hill, S.C. (Scott Kinser/AP)

"They’re interested in whether people are going to be a check on this guy, and roll back some of the devastating cuts and impacts on Minnesota," Flanagan concluded in her answer about working with Trump. "That’s the place I’m going to start."

Flanagan is facing Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter who has turned the race into a referendum on the massive fraud scandal that unfolded under the Walz administration. Tafoya has argued that Flanagan, who served as Walz’s No. 2 as lieutenant governor, should share responsibility for the scandal, while also tying her opponent to progressive positions, including Medicare for All and dismantling ICE.

MN SENATE CANDIDATE RIPPED FOR BLAMING WALZ FOR FRAUD DESPITE BEING HIS #2: 'KNOWS SHE'S COOKED'

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, joined by Gov. Tim Walz, speaks during a press conference, June 25, 2022, in St. Paul, Minn. (Aaron Lavinsky/Star Tribune via Getty Images)

The race has become unexpectedly competitive after Tafoya narrowed the gap in Minnesota, prompting Fox News to shift its rating from "Likely Democrat" to "Lean Democrat."

"The more that Minnesotans learn about me and my opponent and see what my opponent has failed to do over the last eight years alongside [Democratic Gov.] Tim Walz, they're understanding Minnesota needs change. We need fresh ideas, we need an independent thinker and they're jumping on board," Tafoya said in a Fox News Digital interview.

Flanagan has repeatedly tied Tafoya to Trump, whose approval ratings are well underwater in Minnesota.

"Michele Tafoya is all in for Donald Trump — and he's all in for her," Flanagan said last month in a social media post.

But Tafoya appears to be putting some daylight between herself and Trump, as she highlights her support for abortion rights.

"I’m a pro-choice Republican not afraid to stand up to my party," Tafoya says in a new campaign commercial. "When Trump is right, I will work with him. When he is wrong, I will stand up for Minnesota."

Michele Tafoya before an NFL football game, when she worked as an NBC Sports reporter, on Nov. 25, 2021, in New Orleans. (AP Photo/Tyler Kaufman, File)

While the ad drew opposition from some Republicans, including Mercedes Schlapp, a senior fellow at the Conservative Political Action Conference, Trump subsequently signaled support for Tafoya at an Ohio rally he headlined.

"You have to vote for Michele Tafoya, who’s a very respected person," the president said.

Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

#5939. Don’t Go Backward on China Policy

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALI WYNE is Senior Research and Advocacy Adviser for U.S.-China Relations at the International Crisis Group.

RYAN HASS is Director of the John L. Thornton China Center and Chen-Fu and Cecilia Yen Koo Chair in Taiwan Studies at the Brookings Institution.

Nearly halfway through his second term in office, U.S. President Donald Trump has undercut both the United States’ capacity to protect its interests related to China and its role as a provider of regional security in Asia. His undisciplined approach to dealing with Beijing, in which he has focused on building warm personal ties with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and discounted or ignored long-standing sources of tension between the two countries, has reduced Washington’s leverage to shape the relationship. At the same time, Trump’s sustained attacks on allies and partners have driven them to hedge against the United States and strengthen their ties with China. Beijing, in turn, has successfully cast itself as a steady counterweight to an erratic Washington: in 25 of 36 countries that the Pew Research Center surveyed in the spring of 2026—among them Australia, Canada, France, Germany, and Mexico—more respondents had a favorable view of China than of the United States.

Given the failures of Trump’s second-term strategy, many Democrats and even moderate Republicans may try to strike more hawkish postures on China after the midterm elections and during the 2028 presidential campaign. This temptation is understandable: there is a strong desire to provide a contrast to a flailing approach and correct what Trump has gotten wrong. But succumbing to it would be dangerous. If Congress and future presidential candidates reflexively adopt a more aggressive stance toward China, they could both undercut a future administration’s capacity to preserve vital diplomatic space with Beijing and further disquiet allies and partners that do not want to be trapped in a new twilight struggle. Overcorrecting Trump’s China policy would also be unlikely to help candidates get elected or boost their public profile in the run-up to 2028. Recent polling shows that only a small share of Americans in seven battleground states view China as an enemy or consider it to be one of the top threats to U.S. security.

The goal for the next Congress and, eventually, Trump’s successor, should be to prioritize steady competence over performative toughness in dealing with China. Political point scoring and wistful nostalgia for strategies that discount Beijing’s mounting power, and growing domestic support in the United States for great-power calm, would compound Trump’s mistakes rather than mitigate them. A smarter, more coherent China policy—one rooted in disciplined competition with Beijing, patient efforts to build goodwill with anxious allies and partners, and vigorous efforts to refresh the domestic sources of U.S. strength—can make life safer, healthier, and more affordable for Americans.

Trump’s views on China are iconoclastic in Washington, and even at odds with other members of his own administration and party. Whereas most policymakers agree that China is the United States’ foremost strategic competitor, Trump has embraced a narrow conception of competition focused primarily on the size of China’s trade surplus and its export of chemicals used to make fentanyl. He also sees Xi less as a determined geopolitical foe than as a transactional business rival with whom he can negotiate to stabilize bilateral ties.

This judgment—that dealing with China can and should be nonideological and transactional—was also present in Trump’s first term in office. It even survived the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Trump, believing that Xi had exported the virus, empowered senior advisers to implement a hard-line approach to China that included challenging the legitimacy of Chinese Communist Party rule and openly calling for political change. But Trump’s core views did not dictate U.S. policy as greatly then as they do now because he had less command over his own administration during his first term and was less dominant over the Republican Party as a whole.

Trump has also been chastened into a more realistic appreciation of Beijing’s power. China is the only country in the world that stared down Trump’s April 2025 tariff barrage and forced him to retreat. In 2026, Beijing used Washington’s fear of a fresh economic rupture to deter Trump from targeting major Chinese banks as part of his global efforts to squeeze Iran’s economy. Even as the president claims to be ushering in a new era of U.S. dominance, he has had to acknowledge China as a “near peer”—a designation that his administration codified in its 2025 National Security Strategy. Similarly, he has touted the prospect of a “G-2” of the United States and China, making allies and partners worry that he is privileging Beijing’s sensitivities over their concerns.

In some discrete areas, the Trump administration continues to view China through a competitive lens. For example, it is reducing U.S. dependence on Chinese rare-earth exports through initiatives such as Project Vault, an effort to stockpile critical minerals, and pressuring countries to forswear participation in Chinese-led artificial intelligence initiatives. And even as Trump lambastes allies and partners, alleging that they exploit U.S. beneficence, Washington is deepening its security cooperation with treaty allies in Asia, including Australia and the Philippines, and stepping up its training of troops in Taiwan.

Yet on balance, the president has been more conciliatory than competitive toward China. And with his other foreign policy goals—dominating the Western Hemisphere, pushing for regime change in Iran, and ending the war in Ukraine—vying for priority, Trump has devoted far less attention to the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship than many observers had expected when he retook office. His various retreats on China have left the United States worse off: he has undermined Washington’s leverage over Beijing while causing U.S. allies and partners to question whether they should align with a country that prefers a veneer of stability with China to coordinated efforts to address Chinese assertiveness abroad and repression at home.

Because Trump’s China policy places him at odds with much of the foreign policy bureaucracy and the vast majority of lawmakers, including those within his own party, there will likely be pent-up pressure to resume intense strategic competition with China. Candidates seeking the 2028 presidential nomination, in particular, will be tempted to pledge to take a tougher approach to Beijing, potentially including calls to curtail high-level diplomatic exchanges between U.S. and Chinese officials or adopt more expansive measures to limit China’s technological progress. But attempting to restore or make minor updates to the status quo that existed before Trump’s second term—or to go even further in an effort to project ostensible strength—would be misguided.

Most obvious, the nearly decadelong U.S. effort to slow Chinese innovation through sanctions, tariffs, and export controls is foundering. In AI, for example, Chinese companies are finding workarounds to such efforts and advancing their capabilities alongside those of their U.S. peers. Any sustainable attempt to limit technology access also requires multilateral cooperation; as Washington’s ties with many of its closest allies and partners fray, questions are mounting about whether any coalition can thwart Beijing’s technological strides and would be willing to bear the costs of trying to do so.

At the same time, China is widening its lead in sectors such as electric vehicles, advanced robots, and life sciences. Attempting to construct a technological moat around the United States is unlikely to help it regain its competitiveness. Instead, Washington will need to strike a better balance between mitigating the security risks of Chinese investment and collaboration and securing commercial benefits from Chinese knowledge and industry. The United States could gain from using the same technology transfer practices that China employed against U.S. companies starting in the late 1970s, when Washington led in many cutting-edge technologies. In battery manufacturing, for instance, U.S. firms would benefit from acquiring know-how from their Chinese competitors, and both countries would gain if their laboratories pooled capabilities to accelerate the discovery of cures to diseases such as cancer.

The United States also may not be able to pick up where it left off before Trump retook office because even its well-wishers no longer can treat his foreign policy as an aberration. He won a second term after losing in 2020, and he did so more decisively than in 2016. Although U.S. allies and partners would welcome a more multilateralist administration after Trump, they will find it difficult to overlook the possibility that aggressive unilateralism will periodically shape Washington’s foreign policy. Merely eschewing Trump’s crude bullying will not be enough to rebuild trust; his successor must avoid treating allies and partners as instruments of strategic competition.

Paradoxically, though, Trump’s mishandling of China policy has opened the political space for a new, more durable strategy to emerge. Previously, proponents of sustained high-level diplomacy between the United States and China were often dismissed as shortsighted, Chinese investment in the United States was seen as a Trojan horse, and critiques of zero-sum conceptions of bilateral relations were considered naive. But Trump’s actions have shifted the Overton window of what is possible, creating room for a wider variety of ways to work productively with China.

Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress have gradually resumed bipartisan visits to China. Even Secretary of State Marco Rubio, one of the foremost hawks during his time in the Senate, said in September that it would be “outrageous” for top U.S. and Chinese officials to avoid each other. Respected voices in Washington, including former senior Biden administration officials, are calling for some joint ventures with Chinese companies to help U.S. companies develop. And there is a growing recognition in both Congress and the White House that China’s steady accrual of power necessitates a more focused approach to competition.

There is also public support for a new China policy. Although many policymakers frame relations with Beijing as a competition to be won, most Americans regard it as a reality to be managed. In a July 2025 survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, 53 percent of Americans wanted the United States to pursue “friendly cooperation and engagement with China”; it was the first time since 2019 that a majority of respondents had expressed that view. Young people are driving this shift. A January 2026 Pew poll found that only 32 percent of Republicans and ten percent of Democrats between the ages of 18 and 49 called China an enemy, compared with 55 percent and 18 percent, respectively, of those age 50 and older. A March 2026 survey by the Searchlight Institute, a center-left think tank, found that 62 percent of respondents between 18 and 34 wanted the United States to “cooperate with China and improve U.S.-China relations.”

A better China policy will begin by abandoning hollow admonitions to “win” the strategic competition with Beijing. Although China faces numerous internal challenges, including slowing productivity, an aging population, and mounting government debt, it also has powerful advantages, two of which have become undeniable in Trump’s second term: China’s dominance of supply chains that provide vital commodities to Americans and its stranglehold on rare earths that the U.S. automotive industry and defense industrial base need to function.

The next president should neither understate nor exaggerate Beijing’s trajectory; rather, as we have previously argued, Washington should consider it “an enduring yet constrained competitor.” The inescapable reality is that neither country can deliver any knockout blows against the other without doing grievous damage to itself. Both countries will remain interdependent and have to operate with awareness of their vulnerabilities to each other.

If the world’s two foremost powers are fated to compete over the terms of coexistence, they must redouble efforts to avoid a catastrophic confrontation. Washington will have to build trust with rightfully wary allies and partners if it is to shore up deterrence in Asia. It will also have to continue signaling to Beijing a willingness to take reciprocal steps to reduce the risk of incidents that could spiral out of control, such as accidental air or naval collisions. Such signaling will become ever more essential as AI rapidly advances. Protecting the U.S. homeland against AI misuse and misalignment will require Washington to coordinate with Beijing on guardrails for frontier models and reject the argument that such efforts are inimical to securing a decisive strategic advantage over China. The need to work together on AI safety is already shaping U.S.-Chinese relations: at September’s summit between Trump and Xi, the two countries agreed to establish an incident alert system, and many members of Congress have publicly supported broader bilateral efforts with China to reduce the risks of AI-enabled security crises.

Reindustrialization will also be a major project for Trump’s successor. Progress on that front will be essential if the United States is to reduce its vulnerabilities to China and put itself on firmer footing to pursue a favorable coexistence. The next Congress and potential 2028 candidates could outline realistic plans for reducing dependence on China for active pharmaceutical ingredients, rare earths, and potential future chokepoints. They could also prioritize key industries on which U.S. security depends, such as AI-powered robotics and shipbuilding, and explain how they would deploy funding and talent to those sectors. Elsewhere, with public support for the president’s tariffs sagging, his successor could narrow or place sunset provisions on—or, through executive order, rescind—protectionist policies toward China that lower productivity and increase the costs of inputs for American producers. Such efforts would be broadly politically popular at home and would better position the United States to work with allies and partners to push back on China’s unfair economic practices, including extensive subsidies, undervalued currency, and suppressed domestic demand.

Ultimately, the United States must remember that its external competitiveness will flow from its internal vigor. Leaders in Washington should accordingly embed policy positions on China in a hopeful vision: helping the United States realize its potential as a pluralistic, self-correcting democracy. Framing U.S.-Chinese relations around the United States’ capacity to steer its ties with China in productive directions is more likely to produce a resilient approach than casting Washington as a victim or reasserting a policy framework that no longer meets the moment.

Observers can and should debate specific policy positions vigorously. But another harsh swing in the United States’ approach to China would create more policy instability while also discounting the extent to which Beijing’s rise is transforming the geopolitical balance. Taking advantage of the political space that Trump has generated, however ineptly, the new Congress taking office after the 2026 midterms and presidential aspirants looking to run in 2028 will have an opportunity to present a steadier approach, articulating a clear focus on national renewal and a balanced posture toward Beijing that reflects the mood of the American public. Approaching China’s challenge with this sensibility would not only be more prescriptively sound; it would also be more politically sustainable.

How America Can Take Advantage of the Status Quo

Why the United States Should Not Overreact to China and Russia

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Niall Ferguson, Lisa Klaassen, and Eric Schmidt

Beijing’s Green Path to Ending Dollar Dominance

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

The Case for an Economic Security Alliance

Theodore Bunzel, Edward Fishman, and Addar Levi

How Long Will Elites Stay Loyal to Kim Jong Un?

The Arab Monarchies Must Help Washington and Tehran Save Face

Niall Ferguson, Lisa Klaassen, and Eric Schmidt
