#5853. A new cold war: hackers target fridges across the globe

A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, following a cyberattack affecting the French supermarket chains Intermarché and Cooperative U that caused their refrigerators to defrost. Some 150 to 200 Intermarché stores were targeted in the attack on Oct. 12, along with nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets, the retailers said. Fred Tanneau/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

It was a May morning in Israel when employees at a large food production plant watched in horror as the office printers started spontaneously spitting out reams of threatening messages.

Then, employees found malicious code on corporate computers designed to wipe away internal data.

Finally, an engineer smelled smoke coming out of the industrial freezers, only to find broken compressors and badly spoiled food inside.

The company's operations ground to a halt for over a week while engineers waited for new parts to arrive from abroad.

It was all the result of a targeted, multi-pronged cyberattack.

"I do a lot of cyber incidents, but this is the kind of incident that I know will leave a mark on the people in charge," said Omri Segev Moyal, head of an Israeli incident response firm called Profero, which responded to the attack.

Based on forensic data and direct claims from the culprits, Moyal is confident Iranian military hackers who currently go by the name Cyber Isnaad Front, the same group linked to influence campaigns targeting U.S. elections in 2024, are behind the attack on the refrigeration systems. It was a destructive digital strike that took place during the waning days of a ceasefire between Iran and Israel when tensions were ratcheting up.

In the months since, it appears to have become a trend.

Still unidentified hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers around the world. They have spoiled fresh produce and cost businesses time and money. These attacks have taken place on U.S. military bases in August, French supermarkets in October, and at food stores from small markets to big box stores like IKEA in countries including Sweden, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Belgium in early November.

"We're observing targeted attacks gradually built and practiced against Israel, tested in Europe and the U.S., and unleashed [now]," Moyal said in an interview with NPR.

Across the globe, bad actors with access to AI are breaking into and taking control of the aging machines that run global critical infrastructure, from water pumps to cooling systems. That should put pressure on governments and companies to find solutions to long-standing security challenges before things get even worse, cybersecurity experts say.

"With great connectivity comes great responsibility," said Josh Corman, a former cybersecurity official with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency who specializes in public safety. "As we connect industrial refrigeration to the Internet, we expose it to accidents and adversaries," Corman continued. "While these [attacks] hit food," he said, the next ones could go after "temperature sensitive drugs and laboratory materials."

As early as March, hackers appear to have targeted a small chain of kosher grocery stores in Israel, according to avideo posted to social media. In the video, a customer is touching previously frozen food including soft, squishy packages of meat that have clearly spoiled. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the incident.

A couple months later, hackers went after a bigger target in the food production plant and its associated businesses, the incident Profero was called in to respond to. Moyal declined to share the name of the company due to client confidentiality, but described further details about the incident to NPR.

The hackers broke into the industrial controllers that helped manage and monitor the freezers. They also adjusted the safety limits, opened the gas pressure valves, changed the credentials, disabled alerts, and destroyed forensic evidence in the middle of the night. They took advantage of the vulnerable devices as well as the laws of thermodynamics to render the compressors "eliminated," Moyal said. "They were blown up … not like C4 exploding, but they got overused and there was smoke. They were not repairable."

The technical sophistication of these attacks is advancing, in part thanks to AI, Moyal added.

"What we were able to see is they very rapidly were able to, almost like magic, go from initially playing with the system to fully understanding how the configuration works," Moyal said. "They tried the simple things … and then they started to bombard the system with different types of configurations until they destroyed the compressor. It wasn't human, the amount of configurations they were able to try in a short time span."

Replacing parts and recovering from the attack were costly, in time and money, Moyal added.

A propaganda video about the Israeli grocery store hack was released in October. While it was largely wiped from the internet, it was shared with NPR on the condition that the identity of Moyal's client wouldn't be revealed. NPR is choosing not to publish it for that reason and not to aid in the spread of propaganda. That video suggests stoking fear was part of the hackers' motivation.

In the video, labeled with a glowing red triangle embossed with the "Cyber Isnaad Front" logo, a masked man sits in a room full of digital screens, typing away on a keyboard before revealing hacked surveillance footage of customers across Israel in supermarkets that were affected by the large-scale destruction, as well as employees at the company finding the printed propaganda materials.

In Arabic, the hackers claim to have launched the attack on behalf of the starving children of Gaza, closing out with the hacker saluting French students in French, likely a reference to ongoing riots in France over education. It's unclear why the video references French students, though the group has impersonated a French far-right group in the past and targeted the Israeli delegation to the 2024 Paris Olympics. The video was also released just weeks before the widespread digital attacks against French supermarkets, but it's unclear if that timing is coincidental.

Ari Ben Am, the co-founder of a threat intelligence company called Telemetry Data Labs that tracks chatter on the social media platform Telegram, has been tracking this group for years. He says it's working on behalf of the Iranian military.

Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, says it's one of the more technically capable Iranian hacking groups he has seen.

"They appear to have a higher level of investment, a higher quality of activity like actual hacking…they really do much more effective, more holistic operations," he said.

Ben Am conducted an early analysis of the technical details of the hack of the Israeli food plant shared by Profero. He concluded that it's possible that these hackers may have shared some digital tools like wiper malware with other Iranian hacking groups like the Cyber Av3ngers. That group hacked machines in water and wastewater treatment facilities in the U.S. in 2023 to display propaganda messages.

Cyber Isnaad Front, Ben Am says, has a history of hacking into surveillance cameras and promoting their activities across a range of social media platforms, and it's the only Iranian group he has seen use human actors in videos.

"They're capable of consistently compromising actual organizations that have some degree of cyber defense," he concluded.

In August,there was what the Pentagon described as a "possible refrigeration disruption" at multiple U.S. military commissaries, grocery stores owned and operated by the Defense Commissary Agency, a wing of the Pentagon. It's unclear exactly how many experienced outages, though an independent bloggercited social media posts and independent confirmations of disruptions for at least nine locations. Very few details have emerged about how bad actors might have compromised those systems.

The Pentagon has so far refused to officially acknowledge whether or not it believes hackers were responsible for the refrigeration disruptions.

However, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the criminal investigative arm of the Pentagon's Office of Inspector General, has partnered with the Army Criminal Investigation Division's Cyber Field Office and French law enforcement following the hacks across stores in France, according to a statement shared with NPR.

According to two former officials who requested anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation, investigators are treating the outages as a cyberattack and believe some evidence points towards Iran as the culprit, though there's not high confidence in that attribution yet.

While many questions remain about the incidents at the commissaries, there are clues across the internet about vulnerabilities that may have exposed these systems to compromise.

Publicly, there are indications that the Defense Commissary agency deploys remote monitoring control tools for their refrigeration and HVAC systems that could be vulnerable to ongoing attacks.

According to a review of public government contracting documents by NPR, multiple U.S. Defense Commissary installations, including several which have disclosed outages like Fort Irwin and Fort Huachuca, are operating Danfoss refrigeration remote control systems, products that have been identified by French officials and cybersecurity experts from a firm called Claroty as being vulnerable to attack.

French officials have cited those same Danfoss machines as one of the vectors of the confirmed incidents across French supermarkets in October.

According to those same contracting documents, the U.S. Defense Commissary agency is using several older versions of the Danfoss controllers, including some from the mid-2000s that can no longer be updated with new, secure software.

While a spokesperson for Danfoss declined to comment on specific customer relationships, she told NPR that the company is "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems" and "are in close contact with affected customers to support them in addressing their situation."

Danfoss has advised customers to mitigate the risks by installing the latest firmware, removing the devices from the internet, and operating behind a firewall and VPN, Tate explained.

Social media posts about individual incidents on U.S. bases suggest these were not isolated outages that might've been caused by other environmental factors.

Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona that houses the Army's intelligence division, shared on Facebook that the post's commissary experienced "an overnight equipment failure" that resulted in "all freezers [going into] defrost mode." The page's moderator clarified in the comments section of the post that there was no power outage, and that the switch to defrost mode "heated up all the food."

"Trust us when we say it was 'spoiled,'" the account posted.

The official social media account for Fort Irwin, the home of the Army's National Training Center in the Mojave Desert in California, shared that technicians were "working around the clock" to "repair" the systems, and that the outages were affecting bases around the country. They wrote that they were waiting for "temperatures [to] stabilize" before restocking.

Ashley Upshaw, a military spouse living on Fort Irwin, told NPR she found out about the outage online through social media and a spouse forum.

"People were posting that all the frozen areas were blocked off, that there were no fruits, no vegetables. Like everything was cleared out. We didn't know exactly what was going on," she said.

People on base, including those in town for training, were forced to drive more than 40 minutes to go to the nearest grocery store, buy shelf-stable foods from the base's thrift store, or pool resources with neighbors, she said. "There were a lot of people helping others out," she said.

When asked what the military told families about the incident, she said she didn't believe there was any official announcement about a cyberattack but that was what people were speculating about on social media, including on a popular page called "U.S. Army W.T.F! Moments."

Across social meda, commenters expressed frustration that the commissary refrigeration systems were connected to the internet at all.

"You need clearance to even get on base. So why not have the same mentality for other things like refrigeration systems and stuff like that?" Upshaw said.

Following the mysterious outages at the bases, things were quiet for weeks. The disruptions were limited to a handful of targets. It's unclear why hackers didn't manage to compromise more of the 107 Defense Commissary stores in the U.S. and abroad.

Then, in October, a manager of a French supermarket outside of Dijon told NPR he got a call from a surveillance company at four in the morning telling him that temperatures were shooting up in the store's refrigerators and cold rooms before he came to find his freezers practically turned into ovens.

His store was one of hundreds whose fresh food was spoiled that day. The French cybersecurity agency ANSSI is in the middle of an ongoing investigation into what happened, and is in communication not just with the supermarkets and the companies that make the controllers, but also with other industrial sectors "which might be impacted by this incident," a press officer for the ANSSI wrote in a statement to NPR. The attacks on French supermarkets were more wide ranging, hitting hundreds of supermarkets across multiple chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U and Carrefour. Even so, the number of affected systems was actually still a small fraction of the total number of stores and devices within those company's portfolios.

Now, with attacks hitting supermarkets in at least six more European countries, the trend of compromising refrigeration technology appears to be continuing to escalate. Some officials including those in Sweden and Estonia have said impacts were more limited than they could have been, given the warnings they received from what happened in France. However, the full extent of the impacts of the new wave of attacks is still unfolding.

Officials are still investigating all these separate outages, while governments and industries are scrambling to determine whether they're still operating devices that are vulnerable.

Hackers remotely dialing up the temperature in industrial freezers or damaging other critical devices from a world away sounds a lot like science fiction.

But it's happening. Despite a brief interlude years ago when some criminal hackers claimed that they wouldn't target sensitive systems like those used in hospitals, many hackers have since done so.

That's likely because the opportunity to make money by holding critical systems hostage is simply too lucrative to ignore, like the ransomware attack on Colonial Pipeline in 2021.

Meanwhile, these kinds of attacks are increasingly becoming a normal part of geopolitical conflict, whether that's Russian hackers shutting off the power in Ukraine, or Chinese hackers burrowing into U.S. critical infrastructure to provide a foothold to cause damage in the event of a potential future conflict like a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Additionally, experts have linked a series of disruptive attacks on U.S. water treatment plants in August to Iran, within weeks of the Defense Commissary outages.

In reality, securing operational technology, the digital machines that control physical processes in the real world, is a uniquely difficult challenge that has plagued cybersecurity experts focused on it for many years and is only getting worse.

"This has always been an issue," explained Michael Garcia, the Policy Director of the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition, a coalition of government and industry partners working to improve cybersecurity and resilience for critical infrastructure. "We know the threat is there, and it's just a matter of time before a bad actor compromises something."

It's difficult to estimate the full extent of how many of these devices, from remote monitoring systems to what are called programmable logic controllers, are vulnerable to attack and for what reason, though cybersecurity firms have identified thousands of refrigeration systems alone still exposed to basic attacks even after the widely publicized incidents in France.

In recent years, there's been a trend towards greater connectivity between devices, to allow individuals to remotely manage massive networks of machines from a central location. It makes sense, particularly for major corporations who are dealing with complex machines that can't be adequately managed by individuals onsite, unlike a household refrigerator. But many of these systems were not originally designed with internet connectivity or security in mind.

On top of that, many of these systems are aging and can no longer be patched at all, because the companies that made them have moved on to newer versions.

And finally, many of the officials or executives whose agencies or businesses run operational technology have limited to no visibility into the specific devices they're using, which ones are vulnerable, or whether or not they have cybersecurity protections in place. Some of those people haven't invested in securing these systems the way they should.

"Internet exposed devices were always the soft underbelly of operational technology," explained Amir Preminger, the chief technology officer for cybersecurity firm Claroty. Claroty first published a piece on the vulnerabilities in refrigeration technology back in August.

"Devices can be vulnerable to [bugs] that were discovered and nobody fixed them," Preminger said. "They can be known vulnerabilities and nobody patched. And there can just be the fact that there's no security measures. If you leave that door open, anyone can come in and do whatever he wants."

— Eleanor Beardsley and Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

#5851. How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election

Voters enter a polling station at Midtown Mall on October 31, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America hide caption

How NPR makes race calls in the 2026 election

Voters are voting, ballots are being counted and results are starting to come in for 435 House races, 35 Senate races and 36 gubernatorial contests as well as ballot measures and thousands of state legislative seats. But how will NPR call races on election night? Determining a winner in any of the many races across the country is a big job. That's why NPR partners with the Associated Press — and has for many years — to ensure that races are called accurately.

The Associated Press has been calling races since 1848 and even now, nearly 180 years later, the process for making those calls is pretty simple. Here's how the AP explains its race calling process:

Race callers collaborate with analysts who focus on statewide races, such as those for U.S. Senate and governor, and elections for the U.S. House of Representatives. The decision editors on AP's Decision Team sign off on every race call for president, U.S. Senate and governor, as well as races of significance for U.S. House.

Together, they are looking at far more than just the overall vote totals. They study the incoming vote county by county. In states where the information is available, they look at the vote by type of ballot: cast in person at polling places, or in advance by mail or in person. They are also in constant contact with AP's vote count team, in search of the latest information about what's been counted so far and how many ballots may still be left to count.

Once AP has an idea of how many ballots are outstanding versus how many have been counted, their staff can start to tabulate the likelihood of a certain winner being victorious in a certain contest based on a lot of different factors: where the ballots that are outstanding are coming from, what the makeup of those communities looks like and even, how the individual chose to vote.

For NPR's part, once the AP calls a race, we will alert our broadcast and digital audiences on air as part of special coverage and online through digital stories. We also ensure that our hundreds of member stations also have access to that information. We will use AP's data to populate our election results pages so viewers can keep track, in real time.

How are races called when not all votes have been counted?

But sometimes, races might be called without all — or even most — of the vote counted. How is that possible?

The Associated Press explained in 2024 that it uses that same calculation of ballots, external factors and other data to inform its decisions.

In almost all cases, races can be called well before 100% of the votes have been counted. The AP's team of election journalists and analysts will call a race as soon as a clear winner can be determined. That may sound obvious, but it is the guiding principle that drives the organization's election race-calling process.

The AP's race calls are not predictions and are not based on speculation. They are declarations based on an analysis of vote results and other election data that one candidate has emerged as the winner and that no other candidate in the race will be able to overtake the winner once all the votes have been counted.

It sounds simple, right? The AP won't call races until "a clear winner can be determined." But that doesn't always require all of the votes for every precinct for every race. Sometimes it's all about the math: can this candidate feasibly win with the votes outstanding in the places they are yet to be counted? And that raises another, really important point.

The AP – and therefore NPR – will not project races. The team at the AP will wait until it has certainty to call raises and that is why its race calls are trusted by hundreds of news organizations, including NPR. Because they wait until there is surety, even if it means waiting just a bit longer to be sure.

On an ethical note, NPR will not make race calls just because a candidate declares victory, nor will NPR use a concession speech or statement to make a race call either. That is true of the Associated Press as well:

AP does not make projections or name apparent or likely winners. If our race callers cannot definitively say a candidate has won, we do not engage in speculation. For example, AP did not call the closely contested race in 2000 between George W. Bush and Al Gore – we stood behind our assessment that the margin in Florida made it too close to say who won.

AP only calls a race when we are fully confident that race has been won – defined most simply as the moment the trailing candidates no longer have a path to victory.

When AP makes a race call, we back it up with transparent reporting into the research and analysis that led us to say with certainty who has won. This explanatory journalism is as much a hallmark of our coverage of U.S. elections as the race calls themselves.

While election night is the start of these race calls, it likely will not be the end. Counting voters can take a while. Race calls will be tabulated to determine the balance of power in the Senate and the House of Representatives. NPR will cover all major race calls and provide ongoing coverage on air and online of just how the 2026 election shakes out.

#5850. SolSmart celebrates 10 years of helping local governments go solar

SolSmart, a national program that helps local governments remove barriers to solar energy adoption, today marks its tenth anniversary. Since 2016, SolSmart has helped over 600 local governments and regional organizations cut red tape, increase energy choice for residents and strengthen community energy resilience. SolSmart is a free technical assistance program supported by the U.S. Department of Energy and co-led by the Interstate Renewable Energy Council (IREC) and the International City/County Management Association (ICMA).

SolSmart offers free expert technical assistance to help local governments adopt nationally recognized best practices to advance solar energy adoption. With electricity costs rising rapidly and a sixth of U.S. households behind on their utility bills, SolSmart helps local governments reduce energy costs for residents. Solar projects can help meet rising electricity demands at lower costs than other energy sources, but only if local processes like permitting and inspection allow them to come online efficiently and affordably. SolSmart enables this by helping communities streamline policies while maintaining safety and reliability.

Participating communities can earn graded designations by taking specific steps to reduce barriers to solar adoption, such as improving permitting and inspection practices and expanding information for residents. Designation provides national recognition of communities’ work to expand energy options for residents and businesses, while providing measurable benefits. Independent research, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that SolSmart designation is associated with an 18–19% increase in solar capacity per month compared to non-designated communities.

“The city of Athens is proud to be one of the first communities in the country to pursue SolSmart designation,” said Steve Patterson mayor of Athens, Ohio. “When we first achieved Bronze designation in October 2017, we knew this was only the beginning of our residential sustainable energy story. Since then, we received SolSmart Gold designation in 2023 and, in 2025, became the first SolSmart Platinum community in Ohio, the 4th City in the country, and have added over 2 megawatts of solar capacity to our municipal facilities, with much more planned for the future. We continue to see a steady increase in solar installations in the City and know this trend will continue thanks to our SolSmart efforts.

More than 600 local governments across 44 states have received designations through the SolSmart program, in places such as Fort Worth, Texas, Iowa City, Iowa, and Olympia, Washington.

“Local governments are at the heart of clean energy adoption around the country. Policies on topics like permitting and inspection of solar installations can make or break residents’ access to solar,” said Brandy O’Quinn, program director of local initiatives at IREC. “When local governments take steps to remove unintended barriers to solar adoption, the results are significant.”

The SolSmart team is hosting a digital event on October 29 at 2 p.m. ET to share information about its 2026 SolSmart Accelerator.

“The SolSmart program provides free hands-on support to help hardworking local government staff align their local rules with national best practices that cut red tape while maintaining strong safety standards,” said Debra Perry, Clean Energy Program Director at ICMA. “As communities grapple with rising energy costs, increasing solar access can be a valuable way to support residents’ energy choices and advance affordability. We look forward to supporting many more communities, and invite interested local governments to access our free support.”

News item from the Interstate Renewable Energy Council

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5847. Four types of House races to watch on election night to know how it might go

People cast their ballots on the first day of early voting for the midterm elections, in New York, on Oct. 24, 2026. Ryan Murphy/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Midterms coverage: Live results | What to know | Stories around the countryStay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats appear poised to retake control of the House on Tuesday. If they do, will their majority be built upon a blue wave or a tiny trickle? A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.

Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress, and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.

So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:

The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 5th Congressional District (KY-06) and Indiana's 5th (IN-5), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.

Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.

Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.

Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.

Other races to watch: FL-27, NC-11, SC-01, VA-01

In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07, where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10, where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.

New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 could be one of the rare Republicans who holds on to his seat thanks in part to his party's ad spending advantage in the closing stretch against Democrat Cait Conley.

Three of Iowa's four House races, IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 are on the list of most expensive, in part because of the competitive governor and U.S. Senate races that are also on the ballot and driving up turnout.

Other races to watch: CO-08, PA-01, WA-03, WI-03

This year's Supreme Court decision rolling back part of the Voting Rights Act led to many Republican-led states redrawing their House maps to eliminate districts that favor Democrats in a typical election year – but this year is not typical.

Now, the political environment has deteriorated so much that seats like AL-02, held by Democrat Shomari Figures, OH-09 held by Democrat Marcy Kaptur and NC-01 held by Democrat Don Davis are all considered toss-ups at best and favoring the Democrats at worst for Republicans.

In Texas, Latino voters seem poised to swing back to Democratic candidates and could prevent Republican Eric Flores from flipping the seat held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 or Tano Tijerina from unseating Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar in TX-28.

Other races to watch: CA-22, FL-09, FL-14, TX-35

As results continue to be reported, one thing to watch is how far into conservative communities the increased support for Democrats can go.

One race that has received a surprising amount of ad attention is in Arkansas's 2nd district (AR-02), where incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill faces a well-known challenger in Democrat Chris Jones. By the time polls close, closer to $10 million will have been spent in the final months on the Little Rock-based seat that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.

There are also many districts in states that redrew their maps where the Republican gerrymander could backfire, like Ohio. In both OH-10 held by Republican Mike Turner and OH-15 held by Republican Mike Carey, Trump won by closer to 10 points in 2024. They're also in a state with competitive governor and Senate races and stretch between the suburbs and exurbs of Dayton and Columbus with an electorate that could swing away from the GOP.

The margin in North Carolina's Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is expected to win against former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, could determine if races like NC-03 are in play as well too. Rep. Greg Murphy's district absorbed more Democratic-leaning voters after the latest map redraw.

Other races to watch: NC-09, NY-21 TN-09, WA-05

by Jonaki Mehta, education correspondent focused on disabilities and learning differences

Top row (from left): Danalyn Garcia of Chicago Public Schools, Lucie Lane of Shawnee Mission Public Schools in Kansas, Jeff Carroll of Newport News City Public Schools in Virginia and Kaori Anderson-Walker of TBD. Bottom row (from left): Paul Stone of Mount Diablo Unified in California, Diana Swanson of Vail School District in Arizona, Kathleen Tejeda of Alvord Unified School District in California and Emily Ellis of Lexington School District Two in South Carolina. LA Johnson/NPR hide caption

For half a century, America hasn't had enough special education teachers. It's a shortage that's only gotten worse as the number of students with disabilities grows rapidly — 8.2 million according to the most recent federal count, or about 1 in 6 students.

Research explains some of why these roles are so hard to fill: These teachers enjoy working with students but spend more time on legally required paperwork and tasks other than teaching. They often don't get paid more despite having more responsibilities than many other teachers. And because there's such a widespread shortage, the teachers who stay in the profession are often handed a bigger load.

NPR wanted to go beyond the research and hear directly from educators, so NPR senior producer Lauren Migaki and I have been exchanging voice memos with more than a dozen teachers from big and small districts around the country. So far, they've shared tales of joy when a student found success, tearful moments when they felt like they had failed, and waking up before dawn to make sure they were prepared.

For example, Jeffrey Carroll, who teaches in Newport News, Va., said last year, he was teaching students across three grade levels and multiple subjects: second, fourth and fifth. It meant he was constantly running from one classroom to the next. "I just didn't feel like I was teaching, I was never in a class long enough to be a meaningful part of it." This year, he was relieved to only be teaching across two grade levels. "It's been good to support my students in the classroom. I get to do some co-teaching. The lesson plans come to life."

Lauren and I will stay in touch with these teachers throughout the rest of the school year and visit some in their classrooms to get a better understanding of what it takes to do this essential job.

#5830. CPP Wind Engineering develops wind testing certification for utility-scale solar

CPP Wind Engineering, a global wind engineering consultancy for solar, is launching a wind certification program for utility-scale solar projects, which the organization believes is the first of its kind in the industry. The new program aims to improve the performance and durability of utility-scale solar over a range of wind conditions.

The program offers two services. Site Certification confirms that each project has properly assessed climate and site conditions, implemented an effective stow strategy, suitably positioned anemometers and used a qualified tracker or fixed-tilt system. System Qualification is a one-time review of a tracker or fixed-tilt product line’s wind engineering design data and methodology.

CPP’s new program is built from the organization’s 45 years of experience in wind engineering, including wind tunnel testing of solar projects, wind stow and siting studies and forensic investigation of wind damage to solar projects. Tornado risk falls outside the certification program and is assessed separately using a probabilistic risk approach.

“Wind governs how a solar power plant is built, yet there has been no consistent way to show that the wind loads behind a design were derived and applied correctly,” said David Banks, president of CPP Wind Engineering. “Most of the wind damage we investigate occurs at wind speeds sites see every year, and most of it can be engineered out. This program gives owners, manufacturers and their advisors an independent basis for confirming the reliability of wind engineering. Tornadoes, on the other hand, can’t be engineered out. We must predict the probability of loss for those.”

For project owners and developers, CPP’s Site Certification provides comparisions of mounting design options and a documented record of wind engineering diligence for financing, insurance and project sales. For manufacturers, CPP’s System Qualification evaluates the wind engineering basis of a tracker or fixed-tilt product line, providing a foundation for determining its suitability for site-specific wind conditions. For independent engineers, CPP serves as a partner, contributing wind engineering expertise to the due diligence they lead.

#5826. BAAJA gives federal regulators ‘bigger hammer’ to break transmission blocks

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

“I think the cost-sharing elements are by far probably the most important part of this bill,” Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif., told Utility Dive.

BAAJA’s motion to proceed is scheduled to receive a cloture vote in the Senate on Nov. 9, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. It increases FERC’s power by eliminating the federal right of first refusal for incumbent utilities, stripping their automatic right to build new regional lines, and requiring FERC to issue a rule requiring each transmission planning region to file a consolidated interconnection and regional transmission planning process.

The legislation also states that FERC can require public utilities to make cost-effective grid upgrades and determine a penalty for utilities that fail to comply within a timeline decided by FERC — including a potential reduction of their return on equity.

FERC must establish “rate treatments for regional and interregional transmission planning and cost allocation,” the bill says, and require tariffs that allocate the cost of doing so to customers that benefit.

“I think the cost-sharing elements are by far probably the most important part of this bill, and my hope is that can unlock a lot more collaboration as opposed to what we have now, which is kind of folks pointing the finger at each other,” Harder said. “We have seen, at least at the FERC level, essentially no new interregional transmission built in a long, long time.”

“That's unacceptable,” he added, “and it's just not doing the job to lower prices for folks. So I think it's going to make some folks uncomfortable, but it's absolutely necessary to incentivize transmission getting built.”

Chirag Lala, vice president of research and chief economist at the nonprofit Center for Public Enterprise, and co-author of a recent paper that proposed a federally coordinated macrogrid, said in an October brief about BAAJA that the legislation “gets transmission right” but noted that the interregional planning mechanism lacks a “‘forcing function’ in the event regions fail to submit a planning process — only a six-month extension, after which the outcome is unclear if no process is submitted.”

Advait Arun, senior associate for energy finance at the Center for Public Enterprise and co-author of the macrogrid paper, told Utility Dive in an email that in addition to including a “forcing function,” BAAJA could potentially be amended to add “more firepower” to the federal government’s transmission finance programs, such as the U.S. Department of Energy’s $2.5 billion revolving Transmission Facilitation Program fund.

Arun also suggested an alteration to the “federal support restriction,” which currently blocks DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing — formerly known as the Loan Programs Office — from financing projects which have already received some other kind of non-tax credit federal commitment.

“One worry I have here is that there is no money in any of these proposals,” he said about the Build More Agenda. “Ultimately, a lot of the private investment that these suggestions aim to catalyze through targeted streamlining of regulations will still be at the mercy of a temperamental macroeconomic picture.”

However, Harder noted that the U.S. is facing a “lack of fiscal headroom that we're going to have at a national level over the next couple of years,” adding, “I think that a lot of policymakers on both sides of the aisle are going to be looking for pro-growth policies that don't demand enormous new spending."

When asked if BAAJA might be amended in the House, Harder said, “This is a pretty delicate negotiation that's gone on for over two years, and anytime you have something of this magnitude, it's certainly a little bit balanced on a knife.”

Harder acknowledged that tribal organizations have voiced opposition to the changes the bill makes to the National Historic Preservation Act, and there is “some disagreement about what they would actually mean in practice, so I think that is something that might end up being clarified. But … the vast majority of this bill, I think, will probably remain as-is.”

The Build More Agenda suggests expanding on programs like DOE’s Utah Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy, which “has helped demonstrate a commercial pathway for enhanced geothermal,” and streamlining regulations such as requirements for nuclear plant developers to “use specialized nuclear-grade materials … in non-safety structures of a plant where using commercial-grade materials would be just as safe.”

In regard to public perception of the safety of nuclear energy, Harder said, “I think we've come a long way for sure, and I think one of the real pressures is that people see the cost of electricity has skyrocketed. And if we really want to electrify our economy and move it towards 100% clean energy, then nuclear — and geothermal as well, that clean, firm power — have got to be a really important bedrock.”

Some moves from the Trump administration to encourage nuclear development, Harder said, “frankly would have been better in legislation.” He said he would like a “2.0” of the Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy Act of 2024, to “incorporate some of the changes that the Trump administration has made at the [Nuclear Regulatory Commission].”

“But the way that I would characterize it is, move it from a zero-risk approach — where any new nuclear project presents more of a risk than the status quo — to a real risk-based approach,” he said. “You can't have any regulatory agency that doesn't want to build anything at all ... And that's the way that unfortunately the NRC has been for decades.”

#5823. Ireland’s Grid Flexibility Assessment Shows Why Location Matters

Ireland’s electricity regulator has put some useful numbers on the country’s future need for grid flexibility. Its first national assessment identifies about 234 MW and 58 GWh of potential upward flexibility requirements on distribution networks in 2028. Batteries, managed EV charging and industrial demand response could all contribute, but the figures become more interesting at the level of individual substations.

The Commission for Regulation of Utilities’ Flexibility Needs Assessment identifies a potential requirement of 0.6 MW and 3 MWh at the Naas 38 kV/10 kV substation in 2028, concentrated in January. Reinforcement is planned by 2030, when the assessment identifies no corresponding flexibility requirement. This describes a modeled network need, without a commitment to purchase a service or install a battery.

A battery elsewhere in Ireland could provide useful balancing services, help integrate renewable generation and earn revenue in electricity markets while contributing nothing to the particular constraint at Naas. The electrical connection matters. A resource has to change power flows across the affected equipment, in the required direction, during the periods when that equipment is constrained.

Flexibility must affect the constrained electrical equipment at the right time.

The distinction applies equally to demand response. A large fleet of electric vehicles might represent considerable flexible electricity demand nationally, but only vehicles connected in electrically useful locations can relieve a particular transformer. Their charging must also be adjustable without compromising the journeys they need to make. The same questions apply to refrigeration, heating and other industrial or commercial loads.

Timing adds another complication. Naas’s modeled 0.6 MW and 3 MWh figures describe different aspects of the expected requirement. Dividing one by the other does not establish that the network needs a battery discharging continuously for five hours. The duration of individual events, recovery between them and customer operating requirements all affect which resources could help.

There’s an important reality check in Britain. UK Power Networks’ March 2026 network assessment reports that the utility stopped seeking flexibility tenders for certain single-transformer substations whose constraints typically lasted 24 hours. The available flexibility market could not address those requirements effectively on technical and commercial grounds. In those circumstances, reinforcement or another engineering intervention may be more appropriate.

As distribution networks accommodate more electric vehicles, heat pumps, batteries and distributed generation, assessing flexibility at the right electrical location becomes increasingly important. National capacity estimates provide useful context, but investment and procurement decisions need much more specific evidence. The Naas example starts the first article in a series connected to The Flexibility Mesh, an open 99-page strategy report on how physical resources, permissions, operating capabilities and commercial arrangements fit together.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing analysis examines the Naas case, the alternatives available to utilities and the conditions that turn flexible capacity into a deliverable network service. It also links to the interactive Flexibility Mesh architecture.

#5822. GE Vernova in $9B deal to buy high-voltage manufacturer as gas turbine orders slow

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The acquisition of Trench Group will help GE Vernova capitalize on rising electricity demand, company executives said.

GE Vernova delivered “strong financial results” in the third quarter, despite a slowdown in gas turbine orders and slot reservation agreements, CEO Scott Strazik told investors during a Wednesday earnings call.

Total gas turbine gigawatts under contract rose to 122 GW from 116 GW last quarter – an increase of just 6 GW, compared with double-digit GW quarterly increases earlier in 2026.

The company expects its companywide order backlog to exceed $200 billion by next quarter and to have at least 130 GW of gas power equipment under contract by year-end.

Strazik said GE Vernova expected solid growth in turbine orders and reservations in 2027, if not at the breakneck pace of the first half of 2026.

“We certainly continue to see real growth in our gigawatts on contract throughout 2027, but that maybe the quarterly profiles in 2027 are more likely to feel like 3Q and 4Q” of 2026 than like the first half of the year, which saw aggressive growth, he said.

Strazik touted GE Vernova’s planned acquisition of Trench Group in a $9 billion deal the parties expect to close in late 2027. Trench Group has more than 800 utility and hyperscaler customers for its bushings, instrument transformers and coils, according to GE Vernova.

The deal includes approximately $5 billion in backlog and framework agreements, some of which reach into the next decade, Strazik said.

The transaction is poised to boost GE Vernova’s fast-growing Electrification segment, which makes and markets a range of medium- and high-voltage equipment to utilities, independent power producers, infrastructure owners and heavy power consumers.

Trench already supplies GE Vernova with high-voltage direct-current equipment, and the acquisition will allow the larger company to offer “better integrated solutions” while compressing delivery timelines and “enhanc[ing] supply chain certainty for both businesses,” Strazik said.

“Lead times across the industry are increasingly important,” he said. “By bringing Trench's manufacturing footprint and capabilities inside Vernova, we expect greater visibility into production planning and improved ability to align this component supply with our customers' project schedules.”

Trench’s new North Carolina factory will be the first U.S. manufacturer of bushings rated up to 765 kV, “giving us an important capability within our U.S. footprint,” Strazik added.

GE Vernova expects to see continued growth in its gas power order book in 2027, Strazik said.

The company is now taking reservations for delivery in 2032 amid continued strong demand from a mix of about 80% “traditional customers” and 20% data centers, he added.

A favorable mix of higher-priced equipment and a greater proportion of aeroderivative turbines in the order book pushed third-quarter pricing more than 20% higher than in the fourth quarter of 2025 and kept full-year 2026 order pricing on track to rise 50% compared to last year, Strazik said.

But per-kilowatt pricing will likely dip next quarter due to fewer aeroderivatives and more 50-hertz units — which are primarily sold in Europe, Africa and Asia — in the sales mix, he added.

In a Wednesday note, analysts for William Blair noted the lower slot reservation agreements and softer pricing per kW, but said that agreements decreased directly due to conversions and pricing is lower due to “expected revenue mix.”

“While the reversal in trend was initially concerning, management noted no slot exits,” they said. “We believe investors should focus on the pace of new signings … we currently view this [pace] as normalization, not a peak.”

Julien Dumoulin-Smith, a senior energy-sector analyst for Jefferies, said Wednesday that the impacts of GE Vernova’s “soft guidance” for 2027 turbine activity could be blunted if the company continues to deploy cash in transactions like the Trench Group acquisition, which it expects to boost its longer-term fortunes.

GE Vernova’s struggling Wind segment turned a profit in the third quarter thanks to a 16% increase in orders, mostly driven by demand for onshore wind equipment and services in North America.

Offshore wind deliveries also increased in the quarter as GE Vernova nears the finish line on its U.S. offshore wind obligations. In September, the company and the developers of Vineyard Wind 1 announced that they had settled a lawsuit that threatened final delivery of the 806-MW installation off the coast of Massachusetts.

But Strazik and Kenneth Parks, GE Vernova’s chief financial officer, cautioned against reading too much into the quarter’s results.

“We expect to continue to perform very well in the North America onshore wind market, but it's a very small market right now. And although our orders grew year-over-year, that's off of a very small base,” Strazik said. “I'd like to see where the U.S. market goes over the next year and continue to evaluate how we invest in this business for value and/or continue to evaluate how we create value in this business.”

U.S. wind turbine orders neared 3 GW in the second quarter as developers raced to meet construction-start deadlines to qualify for the federal investment tax credit, according to data from Wood Mackenzie.

That credit is now mostly closed to projects that have not begun substantial construction, and U.S. wind projects must be placed in service by the end of 2030 to retain eligibility. Wood Mackenzie expects 39 GW of onshore wind capacity to come online by then.

Still, GE Vernova remains cautious, Parks said.

“We keep saying it's hard to call the inflection in this U.S. market based upon all the dynamics at play, but we will be ready to actually benefit from that based upon all the work that the team is doing today,” he said.

#5820. XPENG L05 Offers A Bit More

XPENG recently launched sales of the new L05 in China and began shipments to global markets. Having seen a camouflaged prototype in Munich a few months ago, I had the impression that it was basically a longer L03. Looking at the production model, other than a few added features and details, that initial impression seems to have been an accurate assessment.

Unlike some of XPENG’s models targeting more premium segments, the L03 and L05 are based on 400V architecture. 3C charging rate goes from 10-80% in around 20 minutes. Overall charge times will come out slightly ahead of a Tesla Model Y (also 400V), but not as fast as other models in China on higher voltage architectures.

In terms of length, the L03 measures 4650 mm, while the L05 increases to 4870 mm. That puts a Model Y in the middle at 4791 mm. The increase in size adds roughly 50 kg to the weight of the L05 across trim levels.

The 58.2 kWh and 71.1 kWh battery sizes in the Chinese L05 are essentially the same as the L03, but the range of the larger battery in RWD drops from 650 km CLTC to 635 km due to the larger size and weight. At this time, the L05 is not being offered with AWD in China, although that might change in export markets. The 183 kW (~245 hp) motor is also the same while the 0-100 km/h time increases from 6.6 s in the RWD L03 to 6.8 s in the larger L05. Both are a little quicker than the European Model Y Standard at 7.2 s. We’ll have to see how the range works out under WLTP.

While the L03 impressed with a larger passenger compartment than the Model Y in a smaller footprint, it did have a somewhat smaller rear cargo area. Of course, because Tesla uses a non-standard measurement for cargo volume, comparing manufacturer numbers is pointless. However, the L05 does have a larger cargo volume than the L03 under standard measurements, which would be even more if measured to the top of the squared-off roof, rather than to the top of the seatbacks. XPENG has shown it holding 9 carryon suitcases with the rear seats up, which should be more than enough for normal people. Overall, the L05 has 41 storage locations throughout the vehicle, including under-seat storage.

In addition, the L05 expands the passenger compartment even more over the Model Y. The rear seats now also have folding rear tray tables and a 17.3” entertainment screen folds from the ceiling. In addition, there are sunshades that deploy to cover the sunroof. Other than the center touchscreen increasing from 15.6” to 17.3” and a few new color options, the interior is essentially the same up front. That includes heated, cooled and massaging seats and an easily visible HUD (European models will likely also get a driver display). Ultra trims include XPENG’s excellent NGP intelligent driving system with VLA 2.0.

List prices for the L05 range from 144,800 RMB ($21,722 USD at current exchange rates) for the base 560 Plus up to 176,800 RMB ($26,522 USD) for the top 635 Ultra SE trim. An EREV version with 1310 km of combined range comes in at 154,800 RMB ($23,222) up to 166,800 RMB ($25,022 USD). However, XPENG is offering a launch discount of 5000 RMB ($750). For comparison, the L03 EV currently ranges from 123,800 RMB ($18,586 USD) to 156,800 RMB ($23,540 USD) in China.

However, a G6 comes in at the same 176,800 RMB list price as the L05 635 Ultra SE. That premium vehicle has more power and faster charging on an 800V platform with close to the same range. And it isn’t lacking in technology. At 4758 mm long, it only gives up a small amount of space compared to the L05.

Of course, those are Chinese prices. XPENG has recently been rolling its latest models with the latest technology out globally. When adding ~20% VAT, 20.7% EV countervailing duty, 10% base tariff, shipping, misc. fees… EU prices would be higher. If the L03 starts at €35,600 in Germany, the L05 could start around €38,000. For comparison, the Model Y starts at €39,900 in Germany (intelligent driving is a €99/month subscription). A G6 starts at €43,600 in Germany.

Personally, I would stick with the slightly smaller and sportier L03 if given the option. For me, the space is sufficient. In some ways, the L03 is a better Model Y competitor because it is not trying to be more than a Model Y. I could also see potential updates coming soon to the G6 to position it as more premium and provide added differentiation. However, If you like the L03 but want a bit more room, the L05 could be a good option.

#5819. Op-ed: Plug-in solar expands access to renewables, but needs a strong safety framework

By Michael Becker, Global Business Director, Energy Storage/Energy & Power, CSA | October 29, 2026

Access to plug-in solar is becoming increasingly available across North America. As more consumers explore technologies such as balcony solar and plug-in photovoltaic (PIPV) systems, these emerging solutions have the potential to make renewable energy more accessible and support broader participation in the energy transition. Solar remains one of the most accessible and promising renewable energy tools being added to the grid, and plug-in solar products may help expand that access to consumers who have traditionally faced economic barriers to participation.

As adoption grows, however, products designed to be convenient and accessible must still be treated as electrical products that interact with a building’s infrastructure. Product design, connectors, wiring, system integration and installation practices all play an important role in safety and performance. Expanding access and maintaining confidence in emerging technologies are complementary goals, and achieving both will require continued attention to the frameworks that support responsible deployment.

Clear safety standards, code-compliant installation practices and appropriate regulatory requirements will be essential to helping ensure that innovation can reach more consumers safely and responsibly. Solar-related issues are often associated not with the panels themselves, but with connectors, wiring and improper installation practices. A major misconception is that consumers can simply purchase a solar panel with a standard plug and connect it to a household outlet. Responsible deployment of PIPV systems depends on several complementary elements working together: products evaluated to appropriate safety standards, compliance with the National Electrical Code (NEC), qualified installation practices, and applicable state and local requirements.

No single element alone can provide the framework needed to support broad and responsible adoption.

An important emerging component of that framework is UL 3700, which is helping establish a product-safety benchmark specifically for plug-in photovoltaic systems. UL 3700 can provide manufacturers with a clearer benchmark for product development and evaluation, while giving regulators greater confidence as they consider how plug-in PV should be addressed within electrical codes and regulatory frameworks. Continued industry involvement in the development of UL 3700 will also be important as the standard evolves toward broader consensus and adoption. At the same time, UL 3700 is only one part of the overall approach. It does not replace NEC compliance, qualified installation practices or applicable state and local requirements that govern the deployment of electrical systems.

Emerging safety benchmarks are already moving from concept to practice. CSA has certified a microinverter to UL 3700, providing an early example of how the standard can be applied to products entering the market. The certification demonstrates how a consistent benchmark can be applied as new technologies enter the market, while helping support confidence among regulators, manufacturers and consumers as plug-in solar continues to develop.

The regulatory landscape for PIPV continues to evolve, with proposed changes to the NEC, state laws and local codes and ordinances aimed at facilitating the safe installation of these systems. As the industry works to establish appropriate requirements, keeping standards, codes and regulatory frameworks aligned with technological advancement will be critical to supporting the growth of PIPV products. Well-aligned requirements can help create a pathway for innovation while maintaining consistency in how emerging technologies are evaluated and deployed.

Technology itself continues to advance rapidly. Improvements in inverter technology are helping make solar more affordable while enabling greater integration of renewable energy into the grid. As inverters become more energy-dense and cost-effective, they can help lower the overall cost of PV systems and support broader adoption. New inverter capabilities can also provide valuable grid-support functions that help integrate more renewable resources and contribute to a more flexible and resilient electric grid. As these technologies evolve, standards, codes and regulatory requirements must continue evolving alongside them so that innovation and deployment can advance together.

Ultimately, greater accessibility brings greater responsibility. As plug-in solar technologies become easier for consumers to adopt, the safety frameworks that support them must keep pace with innovation. By developing appropriate product standards, maintaining NEC-compliant installation practices, utilizing qualified installers and advancing state and local requirements alongside technological progress, the industry can help expand access to renewable energy while maintaining the confidence of consumers, manufacturers, regulators installers and other stakeholders.

The statement “A major misconception is that consumers can simply purchase a solar panel with a standard plug and connect it to a household outlet.” is, in and of itself a misconception. If the plugin systems are safely designed, that is exactly what they are meant to prov ide the consumer–a solar panel with a plug they can connect to a household outlet. The fact that several millions of such systems have already been plugged in around the world without incident amply demonstrates their safety. All the hand-wringing about safety seems to be originating with existing vested interests that stand to loose significant revenues built on the existing over-complicated and over-regulated systems.

Helpful safety framing. One practical reader check is to separate product evaluation from deployment permission: UL 3700 does not replace NEC compliance, installation instructions, or state/local and utility rules, and effective dates vary by state. PluginForSolar.com maintains a U.S. state-by-state guide plus exact-system readiness checks so readers can verify those layers before buying.

#5818. Xcel Energy rolls out $70B, 5-year capital plan focused on renewables

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

“We believe that we can, in fact, protect the planet” while serving growing demand, CEO Bob Frenzel said. The spending plan calls for adding 9.2 GW of renewables and 2.3 GW of storage.

Renewable energy will account for nearly three-fourths of new generation built under Xcel Energy's five-year, $70 billion capital plan that the company unveiled Thursday during its third-quarter earnings call.

The new plan — up 17% from its previous $60 billion spending plan — calls for building 9.2 GW of renewable generation, 2.3 GW of energy storage and 3.3 GW of natural gas generation. Xcel expects the renewable portion of the buildout would cost about $21.7 billion. The plan also includes 2,400 miles of new transmission and $4 billion for wildfire mitigation.

“These investments are critical to serve growing electric demand, to keep customer bills low, to deliver clean energy, and to ensure system safety and reliability,” Chairman, President and CEO Bob Frenzel said, later adding that Xcel “continue[s] to lead a clean energy transition” and believes its commitment to clean energy will attract additional data centers to its service territory.

About $7 billion of the capital plan will go to data center projects already under contract at Xcel. Xcel could spend an additional $10 billion for projects not included in its spending plan, according to Frenzel. That spending would cover the more than 15 GW that is included in pending utility requests for proposals, high-voltage transmission projects and infrastructure needed to serve the 4 GW of new data centers the company expects to contract before the end of next year, he said.

“As we think about future data center growth, our contracting principles are based on our longstanding commitment to ensure that the needs of our customers and our communities are met,” Frenzel said. “We believe in responsible development. We believe that existing customers should not subsidize new large loads.”

To finance the updated capital plan, Xcel will take on $26 billion in debt and issue $8 billion in equity, about 40% of which is already contracted, CFO Brian Van Abel said. The company also agreed earlier this month to sell gas and electric assets in Michigan — including 9,000 electric customers and 6,000 gas customers — valued at $150 million to Upper Peninsula Power Co. and SEMCO ENERGY Gas Co. Van Abel said the sale should close by the end of 2027 and that the price was confidential.

Xcel’s net income jumped 83% to $960 million in the third quarter, up from $524 million a year ago, the company said. Favorable weather, increasing electric sales and this year’s “heavy rate case calendar” all helped Xcel increase its third-quarter earnings, Van Abel said.

A July order by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved a 2.9% annual rate increase expected to generate $211 million over two years. Xcel filed a rate stability plan in Minnesota on Oct. 9 that would freeze rates at this level in 2027 and 2028, as an alternative to the rate case it is due to file in 2027. In Colorado, a September decision by the CPUC approved a 1.7% annual rate that will bring in $184 million. The company expects a final decision on a rate case in New Mexico by the end of this year.

Xcel cannot yet estimate its total liability for the 2024 Smokehouse Creek fire pending litigation initiated by the Texas Attorney General's office that is expected to continue into 2027, according to the company's quarterly U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The company has so far settled 358 claims related to the fire for $410 million; claims by 141 plaintiffs remain unresolved. The Smokehouse Creek Fire burned more than 1 million acres in the Texas Panhandle. Liabilities associated with the fire could exceed Xcel's $525 million insurance policy, according to the SEC filing.

#5816. Ford Wants Utilities To Help Make Bidirectional EV Charging Cheaper For Everyone

Earlier this week, the Ford Motor Company dropped word that anyone with a home EV charger who buys its new Ford Fathom electric pickup truck will not have to shell out cash for an external, wall-mounted inverter for bidirectional charging. Ford is also slashing the cost of its home EV charging and power management equipment. That’s not all. The automaker is also on a mission to convince all 3,000 utilities in the US and Canada to help accelerate the uptake of bidirectional charging systems.

With bidirectional charging, EVs can do something that gasmobile can. They can feed electricity back into household wiring, transforming themselves into emergency backup generators without the noise, pollution, and fuel cost of gas or diesel generators.

EVs equipped with bidirectional charging can also provide ratepayers with more control over their utility bills. With a home EV charger in hand, ratepayers can recharge their batteries during off-peak periods to take advantage of off-peak discounts, and they can use those discounted kilowatts to power their home during peak periods when rates are higher.

Drivers can also recharge at off-site charging stations that offers discounted rates, and ferry those kilowatts back for use at home.

Either way, the home needs to be equipped with an inverter to convert the DC current of an EV battery into the AC current used in buildings.

Or not, as the case may be. As explained by Ford earlier this week, the forthcoming Fathom pickup will come with its own built-in inverter. By eliminating the expense of an external inverter, Ford aims to sweeten the EV affordability pot, and the company has tapped Fathom to showcase the strategy at an MSRP under $30,000.

The missing link is the availability of utility-sponsored incentive programs that reward ratepayers for participating in managed demand programs. That includes rooftop solar, home energy storage systems, and even hot water heaters, with EV batteries being the icing on the cake.

“The opportunity is significant for utilities. But there are more than 3,000 utilities across the U.S. and Canada with largely unique interconnection processes,” Ford notes, drawing attention to another bottleneck limiting rapid uptake.

The problem is that interconnection processes are typically designed around rooftop solar and stationary batteries. “Bidirectional EVs bring new considerations because they are vehicles first, not stationary equipment,” Ford emphasizes.

Rooftop solar and home batteries are commonplace, but bidirectional EV charging has yet to scale up. To help push things along, last summer Ford began strategizing on a scalable interconnection system with the leading utilities American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy, Exelon, and Pacific Gas and Electric Co.

The aim is to get a process in place before the Fathom starts production next year, with a focus on collaboration between utilities, regulators, and OEMs. Accounting for periodic changes in bidirectional technology is another goal

As described by Ford the working group has already settled on the idea that interconnection should be required only for EV drivers who plan to deploy bidirectional EV charging in concert with the grid. Drivers who only charge up, or who only use their battery for backup power as needed, would not need to go through the interconnection process.

If you’re wondering why Ford is the only US automaker to offer bi-directional EV charging with a built-in inverter, that’s a good question. One answer is Auto Motive Power, the California-based power management specialist that Ford acquired in November of 2023.

“As part of the deal, Ford is acquiring AMP’s technology, its team of nearly 150 employees, as well as the company’s facility in Santa Fe Springs, California,” Wards Auto reported in November of 2023.

“Ford and AMP determined the advantage of their technology is best realized with deep integration into Ford’s EV products, which will allow for optimizing both cost and performance while improving experiences for our EV customers,” Ford elaborated in an email message.

You can say that again. As described by Ward’s, AMP had three systems in hand leading to the Ford acquisition. One is a Tesla NACS-compliant onboard charger that supports bi-directional charging through integrated DC fast charge contactors. “It can also be used to tap into an EV’s reserve battery power when the vehicle is not in use,” Ward’s observed.

Another system involves a V-to-X (vehicle-to-everything) power management system that supports grid connections. Rounding out the three is “ampEMU,” an energy management tool that integrates an onboard charger and power distribution system, along with fast charging for up to 500 amps.

By the time of the 2023 acquisition by Ford, AMP was already on its way to carving out an A-list slice of the bidirectional EV charging market. In 2020 the startup announced four new members on its advisory board, including former battery expert Kurt Keltey, who served an 11-year stint in strategic positions at Tesla before moving on to become VP of Automotive at Sila Nanotechnologies.

Sila CEO and co-founder Gene Berdichevsky also joined the AMP advisory board in 2020 along with former Canoo exec Phil Weicker and another Tesla alumnus, Troy Nergaard.

Ford is playing its AMP technology close to the vest, but a poster with the “ampforenergy” handle on the SpeakEV forum in August of 2023 provided some details about the EMU unit:

“The ampEMU is a comprehensive energy management system that manages the complete energy supply chain in an electric vehicle, from the vehicle’s charging infrastructure to battery management. It is backed by ampLOGIC for automotive big data analytics preventing battery degradation and enabling optimizations. ampEMU is compliant with the CCS, Tesla NACS, and CHAdeMO.”

“AMP’s EMU utilizes the latest SiC technology from Wolfspeed to drastically reduce the power electronics packaging volume,” ampedforenergy continued.

“This extremely compact unit will save space and reduce the vehicle’s overall weight, thereby improving range. EMU has the entire AMP Ecosystem in one unit offering cloud connectivity (ampLOGIC), battery management, power distribution unit, and charging solutions highly integrated with each other,” the poster added.

Speaking of Tesla, what happens next will be interesting. Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s pet project, the Cybertruck, was marketed as a pickup truck and it flopped epically, leaving the pickup truck field wide open for other EV makers to take a crack.

Meanwhile, last year Ford suspended its Lightning F-150 full sized electric pickup truck, evidently to focus its marketing program on the mid-sized Fathom, which is entering the market at a more affordable MSRP starting at $28,350.
